#8592. The Glute Training Guide for a Stronger and More Powerful Posterior

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Not every muscle gets immortalized in a rap song, but the glutes do more than look good in pants. Beyond the vanity benefits, the glutes help you do fun things in and out of the gym.

Although the gluteus maximus gets all the attention, the gluteus medius and minimus provide the stability that lets the glute max do its job better. That’s why it’s important to focus on all three, not just one.

Compound lifts hit them hard and heavy, but isolation exercises are necessary to train all glute functions and muscles. You can also load them in different ways: from a lengthened position (think RDL) and from a shortened position (think Hip Thrust).

Understanding those differences, rather than choosing sides in the great squat-versus-hip-thrust debate, is key to better glute training.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gQnMPHoDGEc

Each glute muscle has a different role, and understanding them will help you train them more effectively.

It’s the largest and most superficial of the three muscles, and it’s responsible for much of your backside’s size and shape. Although it’s best known for hip extension and external rotation, some lower fibers can assist with hip adduction depending on hip position, while the upper fibers assist with hip abduction.

The gluteus medius sits on the lateral side of your pelvis, partly beneath the gluteus maximus. Its primary job is hip abduction, but it also helps stabilize the pelvis. It also has different muscle fibers that perform different jobs. The anterior fibers assist with hip internal rotation, while the posterior fibers can contribute to external rotation.

The gluteus minimus is the smallest and deepest of the three, sitting underneath the glute medius. It assists with hip abduction and internal rotation while helping control the femur’s position within the hip joint. It also works with the glute medius to stabilize the pelvis when one foot leaves the ground.

The hip is a ball-and-socket joint that allows your hips to flex, extend, abduct, adduct, and rotate. But not everyone’s ball-and-socket joint is built the same way.

The depth and orientation of your hip socket, the angle of your femoral neck, and how much your femur rotates forward or backward vary from person to person. These structural differences influence exercise selection and positions.

Some squat with a narrow stance and toes pointed forward, while others go wider with toes pointed out. Your hip anatomy, mobility, strength, and limb length all influence what position works best for you. Adjusting your stance, foot position, and range of motion can help you find positions that load the glutes effectively and work with your anatomy.

Your glutes are among the body’s most powerful muscles, and paying attention to your backside pays off in more ways than one.

Glutes give you the horsepower to do the things you enjoy, from squatting to sprinting to other daily activities. The stronger they are, the more force they can produce, especially when you pair that strength with power training.

In many unilateral movements like walking, running, walking upstairs, and single-leg RDLs, smaller glute muscles control your lower-body position. Weakness can show up in a loss of balance, excessive wobbling in a single-leg stance, or your knee caving inward during squats and deadlifts. You don’t want any of that.

Your hips, knees, and lower back are teammates, and when one struggles, another may compensate. Weak glute med and glute min can cause knee valgus, which your knee ligaments don’t like. Weak hip extension strength or limited hip mobility forces the lower back to do a job it’s not designed for. Training the glutes for strength and mobility prevents this.

Almost every powerful lower-body movement involves the glutes.

During sprinting, the gluteus maximus drives powerful hip extension. When you cut, land, or change direction, all three glute muscles help control the hip and pelvis as your body absorbs and redirects force. The glutes also contribute to rotational movements, such as swinging a bat, throwing a punch, and a golf swing. Their ability to produce force and rotate helps link lower-body movement to upper-body power.

Here’s what your glutes need to grow bigger and stronger.

Compound exercises such as barbell squats, Romanian deadlifts, and barbell hip thrusts let the glutes produce force alongside the quads, hamstrings, and adductors, making them an excellent foundation for building strength and muscle.

Deep squats, front-foot elevated split squats, and deficit reverse lunges put a loaded stretch where you need it most. Because the hips are flexed and the glutes are lengthened, they can build greater muscle. Bonus points for using a controlled lowering phase.

Barbell hip thrusts, glute bridges, and cable kickback variations emphasize hip extension as the glutes approach their shortened position, given their smaller range of motion.

Neither approach is better, but both can help develop the glutes.

Hip abduction machines, lateral band walks, and side-lying hip raises train the gluteus medius, minimus, and the upper fibers of the gluteus maximus. These improve hip stability, allowing the glute max to work more effectively.

Seated band hip internal rotation, cable hip external rotation, and seated 90/90 hip rotations rotate the thigh within the hip joint while keeping the pelvis and lower back locked in. Rotational training supports hip stability, health, and more complete lower-body development.

The dreaded Bulgarian split squats, single-leg RDL’s, and step-ups train one leg at a time, improving hip stability. Unilateral exercises challenge the glutes to produce force and stabilize the pelvis, improving balance while strengthening imbalances between sides.

You don’t need 15 different glute exercises, but the right combination of movements that cover their various functions without turning every leg day into a marathon.

Start With Compound Bilateral And Unilateral Lifts

Compound lower-body lifts are the foundation of glute training because they let you go hard and heavy while other muscles join the party. But here’s an important distinction: Many compound lifts don’t isolate the glutes.

Compound lifts build strength and muscle, but moving more total weight doesn’t always mean the glutes get all the love. Squat depth, torso angle, hip position, and exercise technique influence how much work the glutes perform.

You need more than one type of hip-extension exercise because different movements challenge the glutes at different muscle lengths. Romanian deadlifts, full-range-of-motion squats, and front-foot elevated split squats load the glutes when they’re lengthened, while hip thrusts, glute bridges, and cable kickbacks emphasize tension closer to full hip extension, when the glutes are shorter.

Both can build size and strength, and each offers something the other doesn’t.

Don’t get caught up in the Team Squat versus Team Hip Thrust debate. Include exercises that challenge the glutes at both longer and shorter lengths, use a full range of motion you can control, and overload when you can.

Debates don’t build muscle. Training does.

Compound exercises train the glute med and mini, but direct hip-abduction exercises give them extra attention. When they’re stronger, your glute max can go to work unencumbered.

Broad jumps, sled pushes, hill sprints, and lateral bounds powerfully train the glutes and fire up your fast-twitch muscle fibers, which drive many of your gains. These exercises are great if you want your strength to carry over to athletic activities.

Your glutes can only work within the ranges your hips can access and control. Include half-kneeling hip flexor stretches with a posterior pelvic tilt, adductor rockbacks, 90/90 hip rotations, and prying squats in your warm-up to prepare for the work ahead.

The trick to training your glutes well is balancing heavy lifting, muscle-building work, and stability exercises while giving your backside enough time to recover. Here’s how to make it work.

Perform lower-body compound exercises, both bilateral and unilateral, with challenging weights. Maintain your technique and rest two to three minutes, or longer, between sets. Focus on progressive overload without sacrificing range of motion.

Again, use compound lower-body exercises that hit both lengthened and shortened positions, with a controlled eccentric contraction and full range of motion, training close to technical failure. Although muscle growth can happen across a wider rep range, this range balances load, effort, and fatigue.

Perform power movements early in your workout when you’re fresh, focus on maximum movement speed and quality, and rest 2 minutes or longer when needed to maintain explosiveness.

Hip abduction machines, cable abductions, and side-lying variations allow you to focus on the smaller glute muscles. Use controlled reps, avoid momentum, and progress the load.

Single-leg RDLs, step-ups, and Bulgarian split squats build strength while challenging stability. Only progress as your strength and balance improve.

Your weekly training volume should include all glute-focused exercises. Use the following table as a guideline, not a rule set in stone.

Some exercises train several qualities at once. A Bulgarian split squat challenges glute strength, muscle growth, and stability, but you don’t count the same set three times. Assign each set to its primary programming purpose (muscle/stability) when using the table.

For most lifters, two to three sessions per week is a good starting point.

Beginners can split their weekly work into two sessions, while intermediate lifters can use two or three. Experienced lifters focused on glute development will benefit from spreading the work over three sessions to maintain training quality.

Training your glutes isn’t rocket science, but you can make it harder than it needs to be. Here’s what to watch for and how to fix it.

Hip thrusts and bridge variations are excellent for building the glutes from the shortened position, but making them your only option misses opportunities to challenge the muscles at longer lengths and train hip abduction and stability.

The fix: Combine hip thrusts with RDLs, squats, split squats, and direct hip abduction exercises to cover more of the glutes’ functions.

It’s tempting to focus on exercises where you can really feel the squeeze, but muscle growth isn’t determined by how hard you can contract your glutes at lockout. RDLs, deep squats, and front-foot-elevated split squats challenge the glutes at longer muscle lengths, providing a different training stimulus.

The fix: Include at least one exercise that loads the glutes during greater hip flexion.

When chasing the squeeze or extra ROM in a hip thrust, deadlift, or RDL variation, some lifters extend their lower back instead of their glutes. Overarching your back at the top creates movement that doesn’t originate in the hips and shifts the focus away from where it belongs.

The fix: Keep your ribs over your hips, extend through your hips, and stop when you reach lockout.

The gluteus maximus gets the glory, but the smaller glute muscles help stabilize your pelvis, support the ball-and-socket movement, and produce hip abduction. Relying on compound lower-body exercises may leave these muscles undertrained.

The fix: Include band, cable, or machine hip abduction variations to give these smaller muscles the attention they deserve.

There’s one camp that says all you need for glutes is squats. Another camp says hip thrusts are all you need. Opinions run wild, so let’s separate fact from fiction.

Squats are fantastic for building glutes from a lengthened position, but the glutes need more than that, as they don’t challenge every glute function.

The truth: No one doubts squats are great for glutes, but training from a shortened position and direct hip-abduction exercises provide a different stimulus that can enhance muscle development.

Doing a set of hip thrusts tells you you’re engaging your glutes, but just because you “feel” it more doesn’t mean hip thrusts are better than squats for building muscle. Greater muscle activation during an exercise doesn’t necessarily translate into greater long-term muscle growth.

The truth: Research comparing hip thrusts and squats shows both build the glutes effectively, despite their different mechanics. For some, it comes down to personal preference.

Influencers with great glutes will scream from the rooftops that you can isolate and build an upper-glute shelf and a better lower-glute hamstring tie-in. But here’s some fact behind that fiction: The glute maximus has different fiber orientations that contribute to hip extension, abduction, adduction, and rotation.

The truth: Certain exercises and hip positions can shift the emphasis toward different glute regions, but you cannot turn off one area while training another. This is similar to what I explored in the upper- and lower-ab training myth.

If you walk up the stairs or sit down in slow motion after glute day, you might assume you’ve had the greatest glute workout ever. Hold your jeans.

The truth: Extreme muscle soreness usually signals a new training stimulus or heavy eccentric loading, and it isn’t a reliable measure of muscle gain.

Adjust the loads, sets, reps, and exercise variations to match your experience and recovery. Perform them as standalone sessions or fit them into your existing program.

Rest periods: Rest two to three minutes after each superset and 90 seconds between exercises.

Progressive overload: When you reach the upper end of a rep range with clean technique, increase the load slightly.

Manage weekly volume: The full-body workout includes nine glute-focused resistance sets, while the lower-body workout includes 11. Keep that in mind when combining these into your current routine or performing both in the same week.

People rap about and admire the glutes, but they’re the engine that makes the body roar in and out of the gym.

Building stronger, more muscular glutes takes more than hip thrusts and band booty burners. Train the glute max through all its functions, give the med and mini some love, and combine exercises that challenge your backside in lengthened and shortened positions. Include unilateral training, progressive overload, and adequate rest and recovery, and your jeans will thank you.

One last thing. Turn around and admire your handy work.

## Flying Qatar QSuites for 70,000 Miles: The Redemption That Feels Impossible Until You Do It Imagine settling into your own private suite — a door that actually closes, a fully flat bed measuring 80 inches long, a 21.5-inch 4K screen, and a meal service that rivals the best business-class restaurants at 40,000 feet. Qatar Airways QSuites isn't just the best business class product in the sky right now; it's the product that frequent flyers describe as the moment they understood why people obsess over travel rewards. And you can book it for 70,000 American AAdvantage miles one-way. Let that sink in. The same seat — Washington Dulles to Doha, with the ability to continue to dozens of destinations across Asia, Africa, and beyond — retails for **$5,000 to $9,000 in cash**. At 70,000 AAdvantage miles, you're extracting between **7.1 and 12.9 cents per point**. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5 to 2 cents per point. This redemption is *three to six times that*. This is what the FI community means when we talk about travel rewards as a genuine wealth multiplier. If you've been stockpiling points wondering whether they're actually worth something, this is your answer. A cash ticket that costs more than many people's monthly take-home salary becomes nearly free with the right points strategy. The inefficiency exists because AAdvantage still prices partner awards — flights on airlines like Qatar, JAL, and Cathay Pacific — on a **fixed partner award chart** rather than the dynamic pricing it uses for American-operated flights. Qatar, as a oneworld alliance member, is required to make award space available to partner programs. American prices that space at a flat 70,000 miles for business class, regardless of what Qatar itself charges in cash or its own Avios currency. The result is a structural arbitrage opportunity: you're using a fixed-price chart to book a premium product that Qatar prices at whatever the market will bear — and the market bears a *lot* for QSuites. The ChooseFI community has long understood that the highest-leverage use of points isn't domestic economy upgrades. It's premium international cabin redemptions where the gap between cash price and points cost is widest. On that spectrum, QSuites via AAdvantage sits near the very top.

The core insight here is understanding two separate pricing systems operating simultaneously. Qatar Airways prices its QSuites cabin dynamically in cash — demand surges around holidays, business travel seasons, and major events can push that $5,000 base price to $9,000 or beyond. But American AAdvantage doesn't care about any of that. As a oneworld alliance partner, AAdvantage uses a fixed partner award chart for Qatar redemptions: 70,000 miles one-way in business class, full stop.

This means the more expensive the cash ticket gets, the better your CPP becomes — without you doing anything differently. Book during peak travel periods when cash prices spike to $9,000, and you're extracting 12.9 cents per AAdvantage mile. Even at the floor — a $5,000 cash ticket — you're at 7.1 cents per point. Both numbers are extraordinary.

AAdvantage periodically runs "Web Specials" — discounted partner awards where pricing drops significantly below the standard chart. On Qatar routes, these have historically appeared at 50,000 miles one-way for business class. At 50K miles against a $5,000 cash ticket, your CPP jumps to 10 cents per point. These specials are unpredictable and availability is limited, but if you're flexible on travel dates, checking AA.com regularly for Web Specials on Qatar routes can yield an even better deal.

AAdvantage doesn't have a direct credit card transfer relationship with most major bank currencies the way Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards do. Your primary transfer paths are:

One of the most important nuances of this redemption: AAdvantage has a low fuel surcharge policy. When you book Qatar metal through AAdvantage, you pay government taxes and carrier fees, but AAdvantage does not pass through the fuel surcharges that Qatar would charge if you booked through its own program. This can save hundreds of dollars compared to booking QSuites through Avios or Qatar Privilege Club directly. Always verify fees at checkout, but expect to pay $50–$150 in fees rather than the $500+ you might see through other programs.

Doha isn't just a destination — it's Qatar's hub, and connecting through DOH opens the entire Qatar network. A flight to DOH becomes a connection point for onward travel to destinations across South Asia, Southeast Asia, the Indian Subcontinent, and East Africa, all on the same premium aircraft and the same 70,000-mile award. The IAD→DOH route is one of the best-documented entry points into this system.

You need 70,000 AAdvantage miles in your account before you can book. AAdvantage miles never expire, so there's no urgency pressure once you've accumulated them. If you're short, identify your transfer path:

Do not transfer points until you have confirmed award availability. Points transfers are one-directional and non-reversible.

Go to aa.com and use the "Redeem Miles" search tool. Select:

AAdvantage shows partner award availability directly on its search tool. You're looking for saver-level availability on Qatar-operated flights (flight numbers beginning with QR). These will display at 70,000 miles. If you see higher pricing, that's dynamic partner pricing — keep searching different dates.

Availability on QSuites is the biggest challenge in this redemption. Qatar releases award space to partner programs inconsistently. Search up to 331 days in advance — AAdvantage's full booking window. Earlier searches give you the best selection. Midweek departures (Tuesday, Wednesday) tend to surface more availability than Fridays and Sundays.

Not every Qatar 777-300ER flies QSuites. Before you commit, verify the specific equipment. You can cross-reference on expertflyer.com (paid subscription) or check the seat map within the booking flow — QSuites will show the distinctive 1-2-1 reverse-herringbone configuration with double suites in the center.

Once you've confirmed availability on a specific date and flight, initiate your points transfer. Use Citi (instant) or Bilt (1-2 days) if you need speed. After transfer posts, return to AA.com and complete the booking. Have your passport information ready — international bookings require it at checkout.

American Airlines and Qatar Airways are both members of the oneworld alliance, which means AAdvantage miles can book any Qatar-operated award flight at AA's published partner rates. The sweet spot here is that AA uses a fixed award chart for partner bookings rather than dynamic pricing, so the cost is predictable: typically 70,000 miles one-way in business class from the US to the Middle East. Compare this to AA's own Flagship Business product on the same routes (which often prices at 60,000-85,000 miles with dynamic pricing) and you are getting a dramatically superior product — QSuites — for a comparable or lower mileage cost. AA does not impose fuel surcharges on partner awards, keeping out-of-pocket costs to taxes and fees only.

Let's run the numbers on a concrete example.

The Route: Washington Dulles (IAD) to Doha (DOH) on Qatar Airways QR 22, operating a Boeing 777-300ER with QSuites. This is a nonstop flight of approximately 13 hours — exactly the kind of long-haul journey where your seat product matters enormously.

The Cash Price: A business class ticket on this route typically runs $5,500 to $7,500, and during peak travel windows — think spring break, summer, or major holidays — it can reach $9,000. Call it a realistic average of $6,500.

The Points Cost: 70,000 AAdvantage miles + approximately $80–$120 in taxes and fees.

The Math: At $6,500 cash value against 70,000 miles, you're getting 9.3 cents per point. Against a $9,000 peak ticket, you're at 12.9 cents per point. Either way, this is among the highest-value AAdvantage redemptions available anywhere in the program.

You arrive at Dulles and proceed to the Qatar Airways check-in counter, where you're processed as a business class passenger. At Doha, you'll have access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge — one of the most celebrated airport lounges in the world, featuring a full à la carte restaurant, shower suites, and a calm, spacious environment that makes a layover feel genuinely pleasant.

Onboard, your QSuite is a private cabin with a door that slides closed. The bed extends to a full 80 inches. You'll be offered a genuine dine-on-demand service — no scheduled meal times, no "chicken or pasta" announcements over the intercom. The wine list is serious. The bedding is from The White Company. The 21.5-inch screen is 4K.

For the ChooseFI community, the most powerful part of this isn't the luxury itself — it's the ratio. You're experiencing a $6,500–$9,000 product for the cost of points you earned on everyday spending and a small tax outlay. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: maximum experience per dollar (or point) deployed.

Do this: Book as far out as possible. AAdvantage allows bookings up to 331 days in advance. Qatar releases its best award inventory to partner programs at the time of schedule opening — not closer to departure. If you have a target travel window, search at the 331-day mark. Availability genuinely deteriorates as departure approaches.

Do this: Watch for Web Special pricing drops. AAdvantage's Web Specials have historically offered Qatar business class awards at 50,000 miles instead of the standard 70,000. These appear without warning on aa.com under the "Web Specials" tab. If you're flexible with your dates within a week or two, checking this section regularly (or signing up for AAdvantage email alerts) can save you 20,000 miles — a meaningful difference.

Do this: Use Citi ThankYou for same-day transfers. If you find award space and need to transfer points immediately, Citi ThankYou → AAdvantage transfers are instant. This is the fastest transfer path and eliminates the risk of space disappearing while your transfer processes. Keep Citi points in reserve as your QSuites "strike fund."

Avoid this: Transferring Marriott points unless absolutely necessary. The Marriott Bonvoy → AAdvantage transfer at 3:1 is deeply inefficient. You're spending three Marriott points to create one AAdvantage mile. Marriott points are worth roughly 0.7–0.8 cents each, meaning you're paying effectively 2.1–2.4 cents per AAdvantage mile — still potentially worth it for QSuites, but exhaust your Citi and Bilt options first.

Do this: Treat DOH as a hub, not a destination. Doha is Qatar's base, meaning a 70,000-mile award from the US to DOH can be the first leg of an onward journey to destinations across Asia, South Asia, or East Africa — all on Qatar metal. A trip from IAD to Singapore (SIN) routing through DOH, for example, puts you in QSuites for the transatlantic leg and potentially a narrowbody for the shorter DOH-SIN segment.

Avoid this: Booking round-trip when one-way is more flexible. AAdvantage allows one-way partner awards. Book your outbound and return separately — this dramatically expands your availability options and lets you mix partners or return on a different airline without being locked into a single itinerary.

Do this: Build AAdvantage miles through Bilt's monthly rent payments. Bilt Rewards is the only major program that earns points on rent. If you're paying $1,500–$2,500/month in rent, a year of Bilt earning generates 18,000–30,000 Bilt points — transferable to AAdvantage at 1:1. That's a meaningful contribution to your 70,000-mile target from a spend category you have anyway.

This redemption is purpose-built for the serious couple or solo traveler with a specific long-haul itinerary in mind — a honeymoon, a milestone anniversary trip, a once-in-a-while splurge that you've decided to fund with points rather than cash. If your travel goal is experiencing a world-class business class product nearly free, this is among the best vehicles in the entire points ecosystem.

Minimum requirements: 70,000 AAdvantage miles per person, plus $80–$150 in cash for taxes and fees. You also need the patience and flexibility to find saver award space, which is the primary friction in this redemption.

## Honest Difficulty Assessment: Moderate This redemption scores **moderate difficulty** — and that rating is accurate. It's not a click-and-book process like domestic awards, but it's not the multi-step puzzle that some ultra-premium redemptions require either. The difficulty is concentrated in **two specific areas**. **Challenge #1: Finding Available Award Space** Qatar releases QSuites award inventory to AAdvantage, but not generously. Availability scores a **2 out of 5**, which means you will sometimes search for weeks before finding the right date. This is the primary bottleneck. The fix: search early (331 days out), be flexible within a 1-2 week window, and use ExpertFlyer alerts to get notified when space opens. Midweek departures and shoulder-season travel windows (late January through March, September through November) tend to surface more space. **Challenge #2: Building 70,000 AAdvantage Miles** AAdvantage's transfer partner list is narrower than Chase or Amex ecosystems. Your best paths are Citi ThankYou (instant transfers) and Bilt Rewards (1-2 days). This earns a **3 out of 5** for ease of earning — achievable, but requires intentional card strategy rather than casual accumulation. **The booking process itself** — once you have miles and availability — is straightforward on aa.com. AAdvantage's award search tool clearly displays partner availability and pricing. **The encouragement:** Every traveler in the ChooseFI community who has navigated this redemption consistently describes it as worth every minute of the search process. The moment that QSuite door closes, you'll understand exactly why. If you're willing to invest the time to find availability and build your miles intentionally, this redemption is entirely within reach — and the payoff is extraordinary.

Log into your AAdvantage account and search for one-way business class flights on your desired route. Filter for partner-operated flights and look specifically for Qatar Airways (QR) flight numbers. The search results will show the mileage cost alongside availability.

If aa.com does not show availability, search the same route on Qatar's own website using a Privilege Club account. Qatar sometimes releases space that AA's system takes 24-48 hours to reflect. If you find space on Qatar but not AA, check back the following day.

Not all Qatar business class flights operate QSuites. Check the aircraft type listed in the search results — A350-1000 and select 777-300ERs have QSuites. Verify on SeatGuru or Qatar's fleet page to ensure you are booking the premium product.

Once you confirm QSuites availability, complete the booking on aa.com using your AAdvantage miles. The process is the same as booking any AA award flight. You will see the mileage cost plus taxes and fees before confirming.

American Airlines charges approximately 70,000 AAdvantage miles one-way for business class from the US to Doha on Qatar Airways-operated flights. Taxes and fees are typically $30 to $80. A round trip comes to roughly 140,000 miles total plus minimal fees.

Both options cost roughly 70,000 points one-way. The main differences are earning sources and booking experience. AAdvantage miles are earned through Citi cards and Bilt, while Avios can be earned through Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt. AA offers web booking while BA may require phone calls. Check availability through both programs — they sometimes see different award space.

Yes. The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select earns bonus miles on purchases, Bilt Rewards transfers to AAdvantage at 1:1, AA's SimplyMiles program earns miles on everyday purchases linked to your credit card, and the AAdvantage shopping portal earns miles at online retailers. You can accumulate 70,000 or more miles without taking a single AA flight.

Airlines control how much award inventory they release to each partner. Qatar may release seats to BA's Avios program but not to AA, or vice versa. AA's search engine also has known inconsistencies with partner availability display. Always cross-reference qatarairways.com and ba.com if aa.com shows no availability on your desired dates.

Using AAdvantage miles for Qatar business class is one of the strongest partner award redemptions in the oneworld alliance. At 70,000 miles for a product that retails at $5,000 to $8,000, the value per mile is outstanding. The web-based booking experience on aa.com removes the friction of phone calls, and the lack of fuel surcharges keeps your cash outlay minimal. If you earn AAdvantage miles through Citi cards or Bilt transfers, this should be at the top of your aspirational redemption list. Search early, stay flexible on dates, and book the moment QSuites space appears.

Building a company with a cofounder puts you through pressures nobody warns you about, plus the usual startup whiplash. Noah was our co-founder at Alertive Healthcare, our previous startup. He led product, engineering and design teams. He thinks like an engineer. The question he asks reframes the entire problem, and then he proceeds to build the answer.

Here’s the problem he found. Every physician in an ambulatory clinic runs against a clock, and the tell is the glancing. The wall clock. The watch. The timer in the screen’s corner. Patients catch every one of those looks, and they read them. Noah fixed it with an app, and he fixed it elegantly.

Article’s below. See whether his solution works for you. Full disclosure: Noah is a friend. I was paid no cash, no coins, no crypto and no farm eggs to write this. I just think he’s onto something.

I originally built Haptica Timer for my wife, who is a physician.

Like many clinicians, she spends much of her day moving from one patient visit to the next. She is constantly balancing two responsibilities that can sometimes feel at odds: being fully present with the patient in front of her while also staying aware of a demanding clinic schedule.

She did not want to keep looking at the wall clock. She did not want to glance at her phone or repeatedly raise her wrist during a conversation. Even when those actions are completely innocent, they can make a patient feel rushed or leave them wondering whether the physician is still listening.

What she needed was simple: a quiet way to understand how much time had passed without visibly checking the time.

That was the starting point for Haptica Timer.

The original idea was to create subtle vibration cues that could be felt on the wrist without interrupting a conversation. Just as importantly, the timer needed to repeat automatically.

A clinician should not have to remember to start another timer before every appointment or continually manage an app throughout the day.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

Instead, the timing pattern could follow the natural rhythm of the clinic schedule, repeating from one visit to the next.

The goal was never to force every patient encounter into a rigid block of time. Some appointments need more time, and physicians must always be free to respond to what the patient needs.

The goal was simply to give clinicians a private sense of where they were in the visit, reduce the need to manually track time, and help the day move more smoothly without taking attention away from the patient.

The rest of this article is written by Jorge Sanchez, one of my former co-founders at Alertive Healthcare.

A patient is explaining something important.

The appointment may have started as a routine follow-up, but another concern has surfaced. It deserves attention. At the same time, the clinician knows the visit is beginning to run long and that another patient is waiting.

This is a normal part of medicine. Patient visits do not always follow a predictable path.

The challenge goes beyond simply keeping appointments short. It is remaining engaged with the person in front of you while still respecting the time of every patient who comes afterward.

Most clinicians develop their own ways of managing this. They glance at the clock, check the computer, look down at a watch, or try to estimate how much time has passed.

None of these approaches is necessarily wrong, but they’re all rather visible.

Patients may notice when attention shifts, particularly during emotional, personal, or complicated conversations. Even a quick glance can change the feeling in the room.

At the same time, losing awareness of time can affect the rest of the clinic day. A few additional minutes across several appointments can create longer waits, less time for documentation, hurried transitions, and increasing pressure on both clinicians and staff.

The problem is not the clock itself. The problem is needing to continually look for it.

A traditional timer is designed to capture your attention.

It makes a sound, displays a notification, lights up a screen, or requires you to look at it. Those features are useful in many settings, but they are not always appropriate during a medical visit.

An audible alarm would interrupt the conversation. A phone notification could feel out of place. A visible countdown could become another thing competing for the clinician’s attention.

The better solution was a less noticeable timer.

A subtle vibration could provide awareness without changing the conversation. The clinician could feel that a certain amount of time had passed and decide what, if anything, to do with that information.

That cue might prompt the clinician to summarize the discussion, confirm the care plan, address the patient’s final concern, or decide that the conversation needs to continue.

One of the most practical parts of Haptica is its ability to run repeating timers.

Clinic schedules often follow a regular cadence. Appointments may be scheduled in 15, 20, 30, or 40-minute blocks, sometimes with a short period between visits for documentation or transition.

Once the timing pattern is configured, the timer can repeat automatically.

This means the clinician does not need to start a new timer before every patient. There is no need to repeatedly open the app or remember to reset it as the day progresses.

For example, a physician might choose to receive one gentle cue when most of the visit has passed and another near the scheduled end. The timer can then pause briefly and begin the next cycle automatically for the following appointment.

This repeating pattern is important because it allows the timer to support the workflow without becoming another workflow to manage.

The experience is less like operating a stopwatch and more like maintaining a quiet awareness of the clinic’s rhythm.

A typical appointment may include reviewing concerns, gathering relevant history, performing an examination, discussing options, answering questions, agreeing on a plan, documenting the encounter, and preparing for the next patient.

When time awareness is lost early in the visit, the final portions can become compressed. The clinician may have less time to explain the plan, complete documentation, or transition thoughtfully to the next appointment.

A discreet timing cue can help the clinician recognize where they are in that process.

It may provide an opportunity to move from information gathering into decision-making, begin summarizing the plan, or identify a concern that deserves a separate follow-up rather than trying to address everything at once.

The repeating timer also reduces the small amount of mental and operational effort involved in managing separate timers throughout the day. Once configured, it can continue through the clinic schedule with minimal interaction.

During a routine follow-up, a subtle vibration lets the physician know that most of the scheduled time has passed.

Nothing interrupts the conversation. The patient does not hear or see anything.

The physician may begin bringing the visit together by reviewing the plan, confirming the next steps, and asking whether there is one final concern that needs to be addressed.

The cue does not end the visit. It helps the physician recognize that it may be time to transition naturally toward a conclusion.

During another visit, the vibration occurs while a patient is discussing something emotional or unexpected.

The physician feels the cue but chooses not to act on it.

The conversation continues because the patient needs more time.

This is an important part of how Haptica is intended to work. It provides awareness, and leaves the clinician to decide what the moment requires.

On a busy day, small delays can build quickly.

A few extra minutes across several morning appointments may become a significant delay by the afternoon. Patients wait longer, staff members work to catch up, documentation may accumulate, and the clinician may begin to feel increasingly rushed.

A repeating timer does not solve every scheduling or workflow challenge.

It can, however, provide a consistent sense of time throughout the day without requiring the clinician to repeatedly manage it.

That awareness may help identify when a visit is drifting, when it is time to begin summarizing, or when a concern may be better addressed through a separate follow-up.

Even when the physician decides to continue the visit, that decision is made with a clearer understanding of where the day stands.

Being present does not require completely losing awareness of time. In some cases, greater time awareness may make it easier to remain present.

When clinicians know where they are in a visit, they may feel less pressure to mentally track the clock. They can focus more fully on the patient and make a deliberate decision about whether to continue, transition, or arrange additional time.

The timer stays in the background. Clinical judgment remains at the center.

We did not want to create another complicated productivity system.

Clinicians already work with numerous systems, alerts, documentation requirements, and administrative tasks. Haptica was designed to address one specific problem without adding another layer of complexity.

It does not need to dominate the visit or become another screen to manage. The less attention it requires, the better it supports the reason it was created.

The purpose is to give clinicians one small, private signal that helps them use their time and judgment more intentionally.

According to the 2026 Medscape Physician Compensation Report, average physician pay reached $386,000 this year, up 3% from 2025 and enough to outpace the 2.7% core inflation rate.

Eight specialties crossed half a million dollars, led by orthopedic surgery at $611,000. 53% of physicians said they feel fairly compensated individually, the highest share in years. All wonderful news.

However, 61% of physicians still believe the profession as a whole is underpaid, and the average workweek barely budged. 63% of physicians blame bureaucratic work and electronic health records for their burnout. 14% of physicians say that they’re planning to leave clinical medicine altogether because of it.

And hospital systems aren’t going out of their way to ease the situation. Private equity and mergers bring in money that should help expand staff and provide a better work environment.

On the contrary, doctors face heavier workloads than ever with no room for PTO. All to protect the bottom line for those at the top.

Private health systems chasing profit and the policy turmoil of declining reimbursement and Medicaid funding work together to create the perfect storm of doctors at their wits’ end. This month we saw exactly how that plays out in real life.

Nearly 150 unionized doctors at two Twin Cities hospitals went on strike, in what’s believed to be the first walkout by private sector hospital doctors in U.S. history.

This was not a spur-of-the-moment decision, but came after three years of bargaining that went nowhere. The health system had made $6 billion in 2025 revenue but was negotiating pay and sick time as if there were nothing left to give.

The cherry on top? A $26 billion merger behind closed doors.

In case you missed it: The Great Debate of Physician Unionization

Doctors represented by Doctors Council SEIU picketed outside Allina Health’s Mercy Hospital in Coon Rapids and its Unity campus in Fridley for four days starting September 14, carrying signs reading “patients over profits.”

The union voted to unionize in 2023, sat through more than 60 bargaining sessions and authorized the strike with 90% support in July before giving the required 10 days’ notice.

Allina downplayed the disruption, stating that the union represents only about 10% of the physicians credentialed at both campuses and told the Minnesota Reformer that 37 union doctors crossed the picket line while 40 weren’t scheduled to work that week. Both campuses stayed open. The strike ran alongside a separate seven-day walkout by roughly 60 Allina hospice nurses.

Hospitalist Dr. Amber Galarowicz, on the union’s bargaining team, said that the fight isn’t just about pay. “We need to be able to stand up for ourselves,” she said.

Paid sick leave was likely the biggest factor. Minnesota law entitles full-time workers to six days a year but the doctors say they can’t take paid time off when they’re sick without dipping into vacation days.

Allina says its physicians already have paid leave and that it’s in compliance with state law. Never mind the fact that healthcare workers face a higher risk of getting ill.

“It’s become unsustainable for us to continue working like that,” said Dr. Alia Sharif, another bargaining team hospitalist.

Dr. John Wurst, who was part of the strike, said that doctors are also fighting to keep decision-making in physician hands, pointing to artificial intelligence tools that now weigh in on insurance billing as one example of ground already lost.

“We feel like we’re being excluded from decisions that affect the care of our patients,” Wurst said, adding that leaving physicians out of those calls means medical resources won’t end up allocated in a way that actually serves the community.

Cost of living adjustments have been part of the back and forth since last fall. This is amid rising inflation and fuel costs.

Coverage itself is also disputed. Because doctors often work across multiple Allina facilities, the two sides can’t agree on which physicians the union contract actually covers.

Doctors need to spend at least 20% of their time at Unity or Mercy to qualify for the bargaining unit but how that 20% gets calculated is still up in the air.

Apart from this local dispute, doctors across the nation are contending with policy changes that directly affects how much they earn.

Medicare’s 2026 physician fee schedule finalized a 2.5% “efficiency adjustment” that CMS says reflects services becoming easier to perform over time.

The policy applies to roughly 7,700 billing codes, including surgical procedures, diagnostic imaging interpretation, outpatient interventions, interventional pain management and orthopedic services.

Learn more: A Physician’s Guide to Medicare’s Specialty Care Changes — What’s Really Happening?

By law, Medicare physician payments have to stay budget neutral, meaning a raise for one group of doctors requires a cut somewhere else. Primary care physicians and time-based services keep the 2.5% increase Congress passed last year.

Specialists performing procedures have to watch that same increase get wiped out by the efficiency adjustment, and in some cases end up with a net cut once other changes are factored in.

The American Medical Association says that these changes will affect certain specialties more than others. More than a third of oncologists face cuts as steep as 20%. Over half of internists can expect reductions of 5% or more, and the same goes for 80% of infectious disease physicians.

One physician commented that as one of two infectious disease specialists in her region, the cuts would force her to refuse care to Medicare and Medicaid patients or simply retire.

The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the 2025 reconciliation law will cut federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion over 10 years, and 16 million people are projected to lose coverage through Medicaid or the ACA marketplace.

The layoffs stemming from these policy changes are no longer hypothetical. Back in June, Hennepin Healthcare in Minneapolis, in the same metro area as Allina’s Mercy and Unity campuses, announced roughly 100 layoffs this year and cut 100 inpatient beds, citing a $50 million shortfall tied directly to Medicaid revenue losses.

Trinity Health said it expects to lose $1.5 billion to “recent and future government policy changes.” Baptist Health in Arkansas laid off 150 employees, including 10 physicians, while shutting down its nephrology, pulmonary, oncology and infectious disease services.

Allina itself is telling employees that its economic decisions stem from “rising costs for drugs, supplies and labor, ongoing reimbursement pressures, increases in claim denials from insurance companies, and anticipated impacts from federal policy and reimbursement changes.”

Also read: What Physicians Should Know About the CMS Cut That Shaves Your Same-Day E/M Payment in Half

On top of all this is Allina’s proposed merger with Sutter Health, a California nonprofit, that would combine the two systems into a $26 billion operation spanning 39 hospitals across three states.

The merger is under review by the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office and opposed by labor unions who warn that consolidation tends to raise costs for patients while suppressing wage growth for the workers providing care.

Sharif said she doesn’t expect the union to block the deal but she’d like a community benefits agreement that shields against layoffs and service cuts, similar to one recently reached between the state and Sanford Health over its acquisition of a Robbinsdale hospital.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

For those who aren’t working at Mercy or Unity, this may feel abstract. It’s not.

Physician unionization has been on the rise because things that used to work, like individual negotiation, specialty societies lobbying CMS, and professional goodwill, keep losing to system-level budget decisions.

If you’re an employed physician, this deserves your attention. The same reimbursement structure and Medicaid cuts may come for whatever health system signs your paycheck.

Strikes make headlines because everyone has an opinion on them. Bureaucrats like to dismiss legitimate physician demands as unreasonable. But the jig is up, and the people are decrying the monopolization of our healthcare system.

The question is, what will it take to stop the consolidation machine?

Insights on building wealth, making informed career decisions, and achieving financial independence from a fellow physician.

Physician on FIRE and The Prudent Plastic Surgeon share a mission to help physicians build financial knowledge, independence, and control over their future.

Dr. Jordan Frey is a full-time practicing plastic surgeon and founder of The Prudent Plastic Surgeon, read by 20,000+ physicians. For five years, he has shared insights on personal finance, investing, career decisions, and financial independence while continuing to practice medicine.

A Physician on FIRE Partnership As part of our partnership, Physician on FIRE periodically shares select articles from The Prudent Plastic Surgeon with its readers.

About three months ago, I decided to actually give physician expert witness work a shot.

It was something that had been on my radar for a while. I knew other physicians did it. I knew it could be a lucrative side gig. And, at least on paper, it seemed to check a lot of the boxes that I look for in a physician side gig.

And three months later, after a bunch of cold outreach, a lot of conversations, a course on expert witness work, and several actual cases, including one involving a zebra, I figured it was a good time to share what I’ve learned so far.

The first thing I learned is that getting started in expert witness work is not particularly exciting.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

There was no moment where I signed up somewhere and cases suddenly started pouring in. Instead, there were a lot of emails, Zoom calls, and phone calls.

I reached out to lawyers. I talked to physicians who were already doing expert witness work. Plus I joined physician expert witness networks. I introduced myself, explained my expertise as a reconstructive plastic surgeon, sent my CV, and basically said, “If you ever need someone like me, keep me in mind.”

And I’ll admit, this felt a little uncomfortable. We aren’t really trained to market ourselves. For me, there was definitely a little bit of a feeling that I was shamelessly promoting myself. But eventually I started thinking about it differently.

We really are experts in our fields. And there are legal cases where an objective medical opinion can legitimately help a patient, a physician, or both. My job isn’t to advocate for whichever attorney happens to hire me. It’s to review the information and give an honest opinion based on my training and experience.

Once I reframed it that way, the outreach became a lot easier.

At the same time, I quickly realized that being an expert physician doesn’t automatically make you an expert witness. I understood the broad strokes. Review the medical records. Understand what happened. Form an opinion. Explain it.

But I didn’t really know how to structure a case review, what attorneys were looking for, how to write a report, how to create a fee schedule, or even how the business side of expert witness work typically operates.

That’s when I took Amy Fogelman’s High Rock Academy expert witness course. I found it incredibly helpful, particularly because it wasn’t just theoretical. There were actual resources and templates that I could use when cases started coming in, including report templates that I ultimately used for my first cases.

That preparation ended up being pretty well timed.

About six weeks after I really started pursuing this, I got my first case.

Ironically, my first case didn’t come from any of the cold outreach I had been doing. It came from a local physician friend who knew an attorney looking for someone with my expertise.

There’s probably an important lesson in there. You can send emails and join directories and market yourself all you want, but relationships still matter. The case involved aesthetic breast surgery and, to this point, has also been my most extensive case. There were a lot of records. There were depositions. And there were hours spent reviewing everything and figuring out exactly what happened.

Then I got on the phone with the attorneys.

This was probably the first time the work really clicked for me. They had very specific questions, and my job was essentially to do something that I already do every day as a physician: take a lot of complicated medical information, figure out what actually matters, form an opinion, and explain that opinion clearly.

That case is actually still ongoing, so there may be more work to come.

But after that first case, others started showing up.

I’ve now reviewed a handful of cases. Some have been relatively run-of-the-mill. And then there was the case involving an injury from a zebra.

I don’t remember that particular scenario coming up during plastic surgery residency.

But even that case reinforced what I’ve come to think is the biggest advantage of expert witness work for physicians: we already know how to do most of this. We spend our careers reviewing information, identifying what is relevant, synthesizing it, forming an assessment, and communicating that assessment to someone else. Sometimes that someone is a patient. Sometimes it’s another physician. And sometimes it’s an insurance company or hospital administrator.

In expert witness work, it happens to be an attorney.

That’s why, after only three months, I think this may be one of the better physician side gigs available. I used to list expert witness work as something I hadn’t personally done yet. Now I can at least start filling in that blank from experience.

Obviously, the income is part of the appeal.

One of the harder things when I started was figuring out what to charge. Talking to physicians who had done this before helped, as did seeing how others structured their fees.

I ultimately landed at $750 per hour with a five-hour minimum retainer.

So when I’m retained, I receive payment upfront for those first five hours. If the work goes beyond that, I bill additional time. I’ve had cases that exceeded the retainer and others that didn’t. But what matters to me isn’t just the hourly rate.

I’ve reviewed records early in the morning before my kids wake up. I’ve done work during their practices. And I’ve worked on cases in between operations while waiting for turnover.

That’s a meaningful distinction from clinical medicine, where income is about as directly tied to our physical presence as you can get. If I’m operating, seeing patients, or taking call, I can make money. If I’m not there, I generally don’t.

Expert witness work is still active income. I’m certainly not going to put it in the same category as the passive income streams I’ve built. But it’s active income on my terms.

Not every potential case turns into actual work.

This is particularly true with expert witness directories and referral companies. You may get contacted about a case, review some preliminary information, give a brief response, and then never hear anything else because the attorney chose someone else.

Do that enough times and it can become a real time suck. That’s one reason why, so far, I’ve preferred building direct relationships with attorneys.

And once you do get a case, my early impression is that the best marketing strategy is probably incredibly simple: Do a good job.

Be responsive. Be timely. You also need to be thorough without writing a 47-page treatise when three pages will do. Answer the questions being asked. Be easy to work with.

And most importantly, be honest. If your opinion isn’t what the attorney wants to hear, that’s still your opinion. The entire value of being an expert witness comes from being objective.

Do those things consistently and, I suspect, repeat business and referrals will follow.

There is one major part of expert witness work that I still haven’t experienced: Testifying.

I haven’t been deposed or testified at trial yet. So that’s an obvious blind spot in everything I’m saying here.

From talking to more experienced physician experts, my understanding is that most cases don’t ultimately involve courtroom testimony. A lot of the work is record review, conversations with attorneys, and written reports. Still, testimony is different. Being questioned by an opposing attorney while defending your opinions is not something we routinely do in clinical medicine.

When I eventually have that experience, I’ll write about it.

Physician expert witness work isn’t passive income. It’s scalable but requires effort, much in the same way that other physician side income streams can potentially require. And it isn’t something where you send a few emails and immediately have an overflowing pipeline of cases.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

But it does something that I think is incredibly valuable for physicians.

It takes expertise that we already spent years, really decades, developing and gives us another way to use it. And unexpectedly, I think it has already made me a better physician.

Reading cases retrospectively makes you think differently about documentation. It makes you think about how clinical decisions will look when someone reviews the chart a year later without any of the context you had in the moment. I’ve already found myself bringing some of those lessons back into my own practice.

A handful of hours of expert witness work can generate income comparable to working an extra clinical shift. Except I can do those hours before my kids wake up, at a practice, or whenever else they fit into my life.

And that gets back to the whole reason I’m pursuing financial freedom as a physician in the first place.

The goal isn’t just more money. It’s more control over my time. Three months in, expert witness work seems like a pretty good way to create a little more of both.

#8566. The Comfort Crisis

As with many things in life these days, it all started with an episode of the Peter Attia podcast.

In this edition, our nation’s most Badass Doctor was interviewing a guest I initially dismissed as not overly applicable to my own lifestyle. A young,excessively handsome dude who happened to be a writer with a new book out. But the headline of the episode was just intriguing enough to get me to click.

Wow, what an amazing turn of phrase, and what a concise summary of the core of this whole Mustachianism thing I’ve been trying to express for the past dozen years.

While the news headlines cry constantly about our nationwide personal debt crisis or health crisis or any other number of things that suggest that life is so hard these days, I have always seen the opposite: on average, we Americans seem to have a problem of ridiculous overindulgence and easiness in our lives, and our main problem is not recognizing it, and the damage it does to us.

So of course I had to click, and then listen to the whole two hour episode, and then buy the book, and then spend the past month reading and digesting it in small, meaningful chunks like the modern-day chunk of scripture-like wisdom that it is. And wow, am I glad I did so.

The author is Michael Easter, a former writer for Men’s Health magazine was also once catastrophically addicted to alcohol – and descended from a long family line of ancestors with the same affliction.

He was lucky to catch himself from that fall in time to save his own life, and that story alone makes the book worth reading as someone who has stood by helplessly as loved ones battled with addiction. But I think his history with overindulgence in the hollow comforts of alcohol also gives him an edge on writing about the battle between comfort and hardship on the bigger stage of life in general.

So what is The Comfort Crisis about, and how can it make all of our lives better?

The best part about this book is just what a damned good writer this Easter guy is. Like many of the most fun popular science books*, it follows a split narrative which jumps back and forth to interweave the story of an insanely difficult caribou hunting trip he joined in a remote pocket of Alaska, with the appropriate bits of science, psychology and cultural commentary that help us explain and learn from each chapter of the epic shit he had just endured. This allows us to process and apply the lessons in our own lives.

For example, have you ever wondered why the type of bored, rich suburbanites who populate the board of your local Homeowner Association and whine about unacceptably tall weeds or unauthorized skateboarding on Nextdoor are so insufferable?

Why can’t they do something better with their time?

It turns out that there’s a scientific explanation for these unfortunate people, along with most of our other problems:

The tendency of humans to always scan our environment for problems, regardless of how safe and perfect that environment is.

The book cited a study in which researchers told people to look for danger, in an environment which gradually became safer and safer:

“When they ran out of stuff to find they would start looking for a wider range of stuff, even if this was not conscious or intentional, because their job was to look for threats.”

“With that in mind, Levari recently conducted a series of studies to find out if the human brain searches for problems even when problems become infrequent or don’t exist.“

“As we experience fewer problems, we don’t become more satisfied. We just lower our threshold for what we consider a problem.“

In other words, even when our lives are virtually problem free, instead of appreciating our good fortune we just start making up shit that we can complain about instead.

And then our politicians cock their greasy, finely-tuned ears in our direction and make up policies to appease our mostly-insubstantial concerns. And they invent their own trivial “wedge” issues to get us to all bicker about our different cultures and religions, suddenly caring about things that would not have even been problems if nobody told us they were.

And there’s America’s weakness in a nutshell, and meanwhile our strength comes entirely from the times we choose not to waste our time stooping to this level.

Meanwhile, the opposite effect holds true: people who survive in rougher environments than us end up more resilient and less prone to complaining.

In a series of recent interviews, Ukrainian people living in the war zones of their occupied country were asked “is it safe to live where you live?” and a strangely high percentage still said “Yes” – not all that different from the responses of US residents when asked the same question about their own cities.

This adaptation principle also explains why some first generation immigrants tend to build businesses and wealth while their own offspring in second and third generations are more likely to become complacent and spend it down. As an immigrant myself, I can see why this is: conditions were just slightly more harsh and less comfortable and wealthy where I grew up, so I adapted to those conditions as “normal” which made the United States seem posh and easy by comparison. Which made it easier to spend less money and accumulate more.

The trap of pointless worry is just one of the many revelations of The Comfort Crisis. It also gives insightful explanations for why spending time in Nature boosts our mental and physical health, while cubicles and car driving grind us down.

There’s something in our biological wiring that responds instantly and powerfully to everything natural, in ways that you can’t get anywhere else.

Even placing a single plant into a hospital room will measurably improve the recovery of almost all patients from almost all ailments. So can you imagine the power of the medicine you are inhaling if you step into a real, living forest? And what if you spent several hours there, or even several days?

Later, we get lessons on our human adaptation towards the ratio of effort to reward:

And our bizarre natural aversion to physical exertion:

Which is remarkable, given the absolutely insane cost this tendency imposes upon us.

Moving your body, even a bit, has enormous benefits – again to almost all people towards reducing the probability and severity of almost all diseases. So can you imagine the benefit of moving your body for several hours per day in a natural environment, and including heavy load bearing and bits of extreme exertion?

These things are not speculative pieces of alternative medicine. They are known, easily and reproducibly tested, and proven to be the most effective things we can possibly do with our time.

So why, the actual fuck, are people still sitting inside, watching Netflix, driving to work, and then driving to the doctor’s office to get deeper and deeper analysis of a neverending series of exotic and mysterious and unsolvable problems with their physical and mental health?

We should at least start with the stuff we know is essential – maximum outdoor time every day, heavy exertion including with weights, minimal time spent sitting and driving, and minimum junk food, sugar, and alcohol. You definitely don’t have to be perfect, but just understand that these are the big levers for physical and mental health.

Only then, once you reach these minimum basic things for human survival, should you expect that more exotic and niche medicines and treatments are the only course of action.

By all means, follow your doctor’s orders and don’t just dump all of your medications down the sink because of this MMM rant. But at the same time, realize that the stuff that is hard and uncomfortable is very likely to be the stuff that improves your life the most.

It’s all the stuff that Mr. Money Mustache has been telling you since 2012, but with more detail and less distraction. This book is a concentrated packet of advice for solid living.

In a happy coincidence, I happened to be in the middle of some hard stuff** of my own as I worked my way through The Comfort Crisis and I found the perspective quite useful and transformative to apply hot off the press.

Normally somewhat of a homebody, I had embarked on a solo journey for some Carpentourism deep in the mountains of Southwestern Colorado. I had my whole life shrunk down into the new Model Y including food, bed, and the necessary tools and materials to tackle a pretty long laundry list of tasks on two different construction projects (fixing up a mini-resort property in Salida, and starting construction on a small cabin in Durango)

The trip immediately took a turn towards the dramatic as I climbed into the mountains and drove straight into the most torrential rainstorm I have ever seen, then accidentally broke a traffic law in a remote mountain town right in front of both of the local police officers ($115 fine and two points off my license), then five minutes after that had a small pebble hit my brand-new windshield which instantly spread into a crack that spans the whole thing, all before finally limping into Salida to unpack and get started on the work.

“Big deal”, I can already hear you saying, “Retired man experiences two minor incidents while taking a vacation in his luxury car.”

And you’re right, and that is exactly my point.

My life is so stable and comfortable that even these two miniature challenges threw me off balance, and I arrived in a slightly bummed and stressed-out state. But I still knew that in the bigger picture, they are good for me if I accept them as the lessons they are rather than choosing to continue to worry about them.

As the trip went on, more things happened, almost as if The Comfort Crisis book were trying to prove a point. I drove three hours deeper into the mountains and up the steep dirt road to arrive at my second friend’s piece of land – a plot of forest in the mountains just outside of Durango.

My work days in that high desert environment in the peak of summer were hot and physically demanding. It was hard to keep my tools, and my food supply in the cooler, and myself protected from the scorching sun (and a strange neverending blizzard of tree pollen) while still getting the job done. There was no indoor plumbing and we had to be very careful with our limited water supply. And then at the end of each day I had to reshuffle everything and set my car back up as a bedroom and crawl in for the night. Alone and far from home.

But instead of feeling depressed as I experienced this constant hardship, the opposite thing was happening: I felt more alive and more badass with each passing day. I got better at being a feral forest man.

One day, my co-builder and I decided to take the afternoon off and head to the wild, remote Lemon Reservoir for some paddleboarding. We didn’t bring our phones or any other conveniences or amenities – just two boards and the minimal clothing required for swimming. And we headed out into a stiff headwind and little whitecap waves, laughing at the freedom of the experience.

It was hard, and slightly scary, as we got further and further from the shore. Progress was slow even with serious paddling, and we didn’t have any particular plan beyond the spirit of “let’s GO!”

But again Michael Easter was there whispering in my ear, saying,

“Is this difficult, Mustache? GOOOOoood! Then you’d better keep going!”

So we did. And we got way out into that lake, to a point where the water was shielded from the wind by the mountains on the other side. And it was awesome.

We cruised over to the shore to explore a particularly scenic meadow, coated with the softest green mossy grass and exuberantly colored wildflowers, and set at an impossibly steep angle. And damn I wished that I could have taken pictures, but in a strange way this forced me to burn that spot more thoroughly into my memories using my own senses instead.

Then we headed back out into the center of the lake, set down the paddles, and just laid down on our boards to let the wind and the waves take us back towards the far end of the lake where we had started. And what a strange, serene feeling it was, floating on just a tube of air over two hundred feet of cold blue water, feeling like a jungle man with no cares and no plans and no material possessions. It could have been scary, but instead it was one of the best and most relaxed moments of my life.

Eventually, this week of forest living and exertion had to come to an end so I could get back to my own town to be a Dad again. But it ended with a final reminder of the principles of the Comfort Crisis – after so many days relatively extreme work and a relatively sparse food supply, I had grown used to a healthy background hunger. Which is yet another thing that we are meant to experience as humans – being satisfied and free from hunger all the time is neither normal nor healthy.

But when my hosts took me out on the town for a final night thank you dinner at the Mexican restaurant, the immense Burrito platter I consumed turned out to be the most delicious meal of my life.

Purposeful Hardship vs. Purposeful Spending

There has been a lot of talk directed at the FIRE community recently about how bad we are at spending our money, and how we all need to loosen up. And there’s a small amount of truth to it, as my local friends Carl and Mindy recently admitted during a grilling on the Ramit Sethi podcast.

But we also need to keep this whole idea of excessive comfort in mind, and the damage it does to the natural human condition.

It’s great to spend money on adventures and improving yourself, being generous to others, and making the world a better place.

But it’s also way too easy to fool yourself into thinking you “want” things that just make your life easier and easier.

So your job is to catch yourself before this happens, and learn to keep things challenging, even as you upgrade the rest of your life experience.

In other words: buy yourself better tools, not softer chairs.

* Another great book that follows this style is Wired for Love by neruroscientist Stephanie Cacioppo – highly recommended for reading in parallel with a lover, whether new or old.

For me, the questions that help me decide which “jobs” are worth doing for life include these ones: – Would I still keep doing this job for life, even if I didn’t get paid for it? – Does this job contribute to my physical and emotional health? (positive contact with other humans, plus physical exertion outdoors) – Does the job allow enough time flexibility or time off that I can also take care of myself and those around me? (8 hours of sleep with no alarm clock, time to spend with your kids or travel to take care of your aging family members, etc)

If all these things apply, it may well be a good job regardless of how hard it is.

If few or none of them apply, there is still good news: there are lots of jobs that DO offer these things. Especially thanks to the power of self employment.

One thing my family did that most people find crazy is to get rid of most of our seating furniture. We ditched one couch, two armchairs, one chair-and-a-half, one upholstered ottoman, and six dining room tables. We also lowered our table and replaced our conventional beds with wool pads on the floor.

Now we sit and sleep on the floor for the most part. It’s encouraged us to move our bodies more (lots of floor space means room for stretching and exercising) and getting down to the floor to sit or sleep (and then getting back up again) means lots of movement that strengthens our legs. My sister in particular thinks this is verging on child abuse and most of my friends just think we’re nuts. But this is a normal way to live in much of the world; we just find it odd because our culture says it’s not how it should be done.

It was difficult at first, and sure, a nice cushy couch still feels good to me (for about five minutes), but it’s amazing how quickly you start to crave things that require more effort once you change your mindset about it.

Great article, I’ve been following this blog for years but have never commented before. I thought I’d share, as I have always felt that I have the perfect job for the younger mustachians out there looking for ways to challenge themselves in this vein while building wealth. An Interagency Hotshot Crew is a group of 20 wildland firefighters that travel across the western U.S., Alaska, and sometimes Canada to work on large wildfires. It is almost exclusively hard manual labor for long hours over difficult terrain and conditions. It will push most young folks past what they thought they were capable of, and a dedication to physical fitness is a requirement of the job. Spending months with the same group of like minded people doing difficult things with a sense of purpose builds strong comradery and incredible friendships. You get to see many of the most beautiful parts of the country, and experience the impressive power of the natural world. You are basically living for free half of the year, as your meals are provided and you sleep on the ground. I can still remember the first time I ate a low-grade steak over a campfire after working 16 hours, it was the most delicious meal I’ve ever had. “Hunger is the best seasoning”, as one of my crewmembers liked to put it. After a long season (1000 + hours of overtime), newer folks get the entire winter off. If you leverage your free time and fire checks wisely, you can drastically improve your situation while staying debt free. I was able to finish college, do some travelling, and build my house, all while saving money. It’s definitely not for everyone, and I don’t know if I would recommend it for a long career as the schedule doesn’t lend itself to a very balanced lifestyle. But for someone in their 20s looking to challenge themselves, I’ve always felt it is an amazing job.

Interesting conversation. One thing I didn’t see anyone mention is the fact that humans, like virtually all other mammals, are hard-wired to do as little as possible outside of the necessities (finding food, shelter, fornicating, fighting enemies) because energy expended on activities not related to those necessary for survival may just cost one their survival, at least in the “old days” of the jungle. The same evolutionary factors that make our bodies not want to shed fat or what to eat (sweet, not bitter) are in play when deciding whether to take the stairs or the escalator. It’s highly likely that without the default of lazy that most of what makes up civilization wouldn’t exist, since virtually everything we’ve ever invented beyond ensuring basic survival has been to reduce energy expenditure. Why walk when you can drive? Why forage when you can farm? ETC.

So the human animal has to consciously make the decision to do that which goes against his/her basic instincts.

A great book about it: “Exercised: The Science of Physical Activity, Rest and Health”, by Daniel E. Lieberman.
