The simplest high-value card perk in travel rewards — no points math required

Picture this: you walk into a stunning hotel lobby — maybe it's the Hyatt Regency Kyoto, maybe it's the Andaz Maui at Wailea, maybe it's a chic Hyatt Centric in the heart of a city you've always wanted to explore. You hand over your World of Hyatt card at check-in, and the night is on the house. Not because you're a high roller. Not because you spent $50,000 on a credit card. Because you crossed a spending threshold you were hitting anyway, and Hyatt rewarded you with a free night certificate that covers any Category 1–4 property in the entire portfolio. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about travel rewards done right: identifying the moments where a credit card benefit perfectly intersects with your normal life, and extracting maximum value with minimum complexity. ## The Math That Makes This a No-Brainer Here's the value proposition in plain numbers. Category 4 Hyatt properties — places like the Thompson Nashville, the Hyatt Regency Maui, or the Andaz San Diego — regularly command **$200 to $400 per night** in cash. On peak dates, holiday weekends, or in premium markets, that number climbs even higher. Your free night certificate covers any of these properties at no additional points cost. None. Zero. This isn't a discount. It's a full, unrestricted free night at properties that charge real-world luxury rates. Why does this represent a genuine pricing inefficiency? Because Hyatt's Category 1–4 certificates are earned through a flat spending threshold — $15,000 on the World of Hyatt Credit Card in a calendar year — and can be redeemed at properties whose nightly rates vary enormously. A Category 4 certificate costs the same to earn whether you use it at a $150 roadside property or a $400 resort. The system rewards you for targeting the high end of the range every single time. For a household already putting everyday spending on a rewards card, $15,000 across a full calendar year is often an achievable benchmark. Groceries, utilities, insurance premiums, quarterly tax payments — it adds up faster than you think. And when it does, Hyatt drops a certificate in your account that can deliver **$300–$400 in hotel value** without spending a single additional point. In the World of Hyatt program — consistently rated the **best hotel loyalty program for value per point** — this certificate is one of the most quietly powerful perks on any hotel card in the market.

The core mechanism here isn't a transfer partnership exploit or a routing rule loophole. It's simpler and more durable than that: Hyatt's Category system creates a ceiling, not a floor. When you earn a Category 1–4 free night certificate, you're not locked into a $150-a-night budget motel. You're handed a key that opens any door in that range — and some of those doors lead to genuinely spectacular properties.

Hyatt operates on a fixed award chart, ranging from 3,500 points for a Category 1 night all the way up to 45,000 points for a Category 8 night. Unlike programs that use dynamic pricing (where award costs swing with cash demand), Hyatt's chart is static. A Category 4 property costs the same 15,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in February or New Year's Eve.

Your free night certificate functions exactly like those 15,000 points — but you earned it through card spending, not through a points balance. This means the certificate has a defined and predictable value: whatever a Category 4 property charges in cash on the night you use it is exactly what you're getting for free.

The pricing inefficiency exists because Hyatt assigns categories based on average nightly rates across the year — but peak-season rates at desirable Category 4 properties can blow well past that average. A Hyatt Regency in a major city might be Category 4 because its average annual rate qualifies, but on a conference weekend or holiday weekend, that same room might cost $350–$400. Your certificate captures that peak-season value without any upcharge.

While this sweet spot is certificate-based (no points required), World of Hyatt integrates beautifully with two major transferable currency programs:

This matters for your broader strategy. If you want to stack a certificate with a separate points redemption — say, booking multiple nights where the first is covered by the certificate and subsequent nights use transferred points — you have two strong, flexible on-ramps into the Hyatt ecosystem. Chase Ultimate Rewards is the workhorse of the FI community's travel rewards stack, and having Hyatt as an instant 1:1 partner makes it one of the most actionable transfer relationships in the game.

Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award redemptions — a meaningful distinction compared to some airline programs where surcharges can swallow most of your savings. Your certificate redemption is clean: one certificate, one free night, no surprise fees at checkout beyond standard resort fees (which, to be fair, do apply at some properties — more on that in Pro Tips).

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. As a World of Hyatt Credit Card holder, your card activity will naturally keep your account active, so expiry is rarely a concern for cardholders. But if you ever cancel the card, make sure you use your points and certificates before they age out.

Booking a World of Hyatt free night certificate is genuinely one of the easiest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's the complete walkthrough from certificate to check-in.

Log in to your World of Hyatt account at hyatt.com and navigate to your account dashboard. Under the "My Certificates & Awards" section, confirm your Category 1–4 free night certificate is present and note its expiration date. Certificates are typically valid for 12 months from issuance, so don't let it sit unused. If you don't see it and you've crossed the $15,000 annual spend threshold on your World of Hyatt Credit Card, allow a few days for it to post after your statement closes, or call Chase to confirm.

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search function. You can filter by World of Hyatt category — specifically, search for Category 4 properties in any destination you're targeting. Don't shortchange yourself by defaulting to a Category 1 or 2 property out of habit. The certificate works at any Category 1–4 property, so always target the top of the range. Look for properties with high nightly cash rates — this is where your certificate delivers the most value.

Once you've identified a target property, search your dates on hyatt.com and switch the search to "Use Points." Category 4 properties will show award availability for 15,000 points per night. If award availability shows for that date, your certificate will cover it. Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance, so for peak travel dates — holidays, major events, popular travel seasons — you can and should book the maximum window out.

Proceed through the booking process. At the payment step, you'll see an option to "Apply Free Night Award" or select your certificate from your account. Select the Category 1–4 certificate. The system will apply it and your total cash charge drops to $0 for the room rate (plus taxes and any applicable resort fees).

Hyatt award availability at popular properties can be limited during peak periods. Your tactical options:

Hyatt operates on a fixed category system where each property is assigned a category from 1 to 8 based on the brand and location, not the current market rate. This creates a structural pricing inefficiency: a Category 4 property in a high-demand market like Maui or Kyoto charges the same certificate cost as a Category 4 in a mid-tier city. Your free night certificate works at all of them equally. Unlike hotel programs with dynamic pricing where the cost of a free night fluctuates with demand, Hyatt's fixed chart means you can target the highest-value Category 4 properties without paying more. The card's $95 annual fee is one of the lowest in the premium hotel card category, yet the certificate alone delivers $250 to $400 or more in value — a return that makes the math trivially easy for any FI-minded household.

This sweet spot is built for the everyday FI household that's already spending $15,000 or more annually on a single credit card and wants to redirect that activity toward a meaningful travel benefit. You don't need a large points balance. You don't need to understand transfer partners or award chart math. You earn the certificate by spending, you apply it at checkout, and you get a free night at a genuinely nice hotel.

You need: the World of Hyatt Credit Card, $15,000 in annual card spending, and a World of Hyatt account. No minimum points balance required — this is a card perk, not a points redemption.

If your annual spending is significantly below $15,000 on a single card, this particular mechanism won't trigger. In that case, the World of Hyatt Credit Card still earns Hyatt points on spending and delivers a Category 1–4 certificate on each card anniversary — so it retains value, just through a different path. Also, if you're deeply committed to a non-Hyatt hotel program, the benefit is obviously less useful without a library of Hyatt properties in your regular rotation.

## Rated: Easy (4/5 Beginner Friendly) This is one of the most accessible sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem, and that's by design. The certificate mechanism removes the two biggest friction points in traditional points redemptions: **finding the right number of points** and **navigating complex transfer timing**. You earn the certificate passively through spending, it posts to your account automatically, and the booking process on hyatt.com is as intuitive as booking any other hotel stay. ## What Makes It Easy - **No transfer required** — the certificate lives in your World of Hyatt account, ready to apply at checkout - **Fixed pricing** — Category 4 is Category 4 everywhere in the world; no dynamic pricing surprises - **Simple availability search** — hyatt.com's award search is clean and straightforward ## The One Genuine Challenge: Availability at Popular Properties The only real friction point is award inventory at high-demand Category 4 properties on desirable dates. Hyatt limits how many award rooms it releases per night, and popular properties in destinations like Hawaii or New York fill quickly. **Three ways to beat this:** 1. Search 395 days in advance when fresh inventory releases 2. Build a shortlist of 3–5 Category 4 properties in your target region so you have backup options 3. Stay flexible on dates — midweek nights almost always have more award availability than weekends If you can approach this with even modest date flexibility, you will find great options. The Hyatt portfolio at Category 4 is large and geographically diverse, and there is almost always a compelling property available somewhere you'd actually want to go. For anyone new to travel rewards, this certificate is the perfect first redemption — low complexity, high reward, and a genuinely memorable hotel stay to show your household what this strategy can deliver.

#8472. A Stock Is a Slice of Future Profits – Own Hundreds Through One Fund

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Buying a share of stock makes you a part owner of a company. You earn as its profits grow, through a rising share price and, at many companies, a cash dividend. You can’t lose more than you paid, but one company’s stock can still go to zero. Start with a fund that holds hundreds of companies.

Your shares come with a claim on the company’s profits and a vote, usually one per share, on matters like who sits on its board of directors, the group that oversees its managers. They give you no say in how the business is run day to day, and no promise of a dividend or a rising price.

A share’s price depends on what investors expect the company to earn in the years ahead, not on what it earned last year. That’s why a stock can fall while the business is doing fine. A company can beat analysts’ forecasts for the quarter and still see its shares drop if its outlook disappoints.

Shareholders are also paid last when a company goes bankrupt. Its lenders, suppliers, and employees are paid before you are, and the shares are usually left worthless. The debts it can’t pay never become yours, though, because a corporation is legally separate from its owners.

Put $1,000 into a single company’s stock and you can lose all of it, as shareholders in Lehman Brothers and Enron did when both went bankrupt and their stock was canceled. Put the same $1,000 into an S&P 500 index fund, which owns shares of about 500 large U.S. companies, and one bankruptcy costs you only a small part of it.

You don’t need to pick the next big winner to profit from stocks. The fund gives you a slice of hundreds of companies’ profits, and you can buy it through a brokerage account, the same kind of account you’d use for a single stock.

Make an S&P 500 index fund your first purchase, and buy individual stocks later only with money you could afford to lose.

Systeme.io has burst onto the digital marketing scene, brandishing a bold claim as an all-in-one, free platform.

Let’s face it, when you hear something like that, your first thought is, “This has got to be too good to be true.”

That was my initial reaction too. A free, do-it-all software that doesn’t suck? Highly doubtful.

But here’s the shocker: Systeme.io isn’t just blowing smoke. It’s a game-changer. As someone who’s navigated the maze of digital marketing tools, I was prepared for disappointment. Yet, Systeme.io left me floored with its capabilities.

#8468. Trekking and Packrafting 700Km Across Northern Siberia

Two Russian explorers have completed a journey of about 700km across the remote Putorana Plateau in northern Siberia. During their expedition, they encountered drought conditions, wildfires, and a brazen bear that raided their food supplies.

Danil Barashkov and Sergey Malykh set off in early July. They flew to the small town of Svetlogorsk in northern Siberia, before taking a motorboat up the Kureika River system toward Lake Dupkun. On July 7, they started on foot across the Putorana Plateau from a nearby scientific research base.

A mountainous region between 67°N and 70°N in the Arctic Circle, the plateau is the size of Great Britain. Featuring some 25,000 lakes, it is the second-largest store of fresh water in Russia after Lake Baikal. The men set out with 40kg packs and entered the plateau’s remote eastern section, expecting to use packrafts for most of their journey. Instead, they found drought conditions, with water levels too low to paddle, and even drinking water in short supply.

“There was almost no rain all of June. So we ended up like this: ‘I’m standing on the pavement, wearing skis.’ We arrived with our packrafts, and there was no water,” Malykh told Russian news site NGS24.RU. Though water was scarce, the mosquitoes remained. “I’ve never seen anything like this before: you lift the lid of the pot, and there’s a layer of mosquitoes floating around. Yeah, we definitely had no problem with protein.”

The pair found very dry conditions early in their trip. Photo: Danil Barashkov

Their original plan was to cross the plateau and continue to the settlement of Khatanga in northern Siberia. However, the exceptionally dry conditions forced a change of plan. Instead, they crossed toward the upper basin of the Kotuy River, 300km of hiking that sometimes required shuttles to move their gear. They covered only 15km per day and realized that their trip would run longer than their initial six-week plan. But this slog paid off; from the Kotuy, they could finally use their packrafts.

Barashkov and Malykh had a few scary bear encounters. In one instance, they almost walked into a sleeping bear, and in another, a curious bear only retreated from their campsite after coming as close as 15 meters — and after ignoring their shouts and a shot from a flare gun.

A bear that didn’t come too close. Photo: Danil Barashkov

However, the worst instance came after they cached some food. A bear had found the supplies and was still eating them when they returned. With hundreds of kilometers still to travel, Barashkov and Malykh couldn’t afford to lose everything. They collected their bear deterrents and managed to briefly scare the bear away before hurriedly packing what remained of their food into their backpacks and escaping downwind.

Over the next three weeks, they used packrafts to travel 400km and their luck improved. They found plentiful berries and caught fish in the river to supplement their remaining food.

Their arrival at Chirinda in the second half of August marked the end of their expedition after around 60 days. Yet forest fires forced the pair to remain in the village for another 10 days. Wildfires swept through the surrounding tundra forests and smothered the area in smoke, grounding flights.

Wildfire smoke near the village of Chirinda. Photo: Danil Barashkov

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8466. Russian Team Moving Up on Everest

The only team currently on Everest has set off across an untouched Khumbu Icefall. There are no ladders or ropes at this time of year, and everything ahead of them is uncertain.

Earlier this week, the Russian team of Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shipilov, and Natalya Belyankina acclimatized toward the Nuptse shoulder, to the right of the Khumbu Icefall. Heavy snow slowed them, eventually forcing them to stop for the night at 5,650m.

Nuptse in the sun, with the Khumbu Glacier at the base and Everest’s West Shoulder on the left. Photo: Russian Everest Expedition 2026

Returning to their quarters in Lobuche, the team focused on rest and pondered their options. “We are considering two alternatives: either going up across the Khumbu Icefall or trying the West Ridge via the Lho La, the mountain pass to the left of the Khumbu Glacier that leads to Everest’s west ridge,” they said. Jost Kobusch has attempted the West Ride/Lho La route several times in winter.

The Russians have now chosen the first option. “We’re heading up, attempting to get through the Khumbu Icefall,” Vasilief told Mountainclub. “We’ll see how things go from there.”

The team plans to spend six days on the mountain and has not confirmed whether they will attempt the summit or complete another partial trip.

#8464. Types of Investments – Know Whether You’re Buying Ownership or a Loan

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Nearly every investment makes you an owner or a lender. Owning stocks or property can grow your money but can fall hard, while lending through bonds and bank CDs pays interest and swings less. Before you buy anything, name which one it is and what would make it lose value.

A product’s name won’t always tell you which one you’re buying. A brokerage menu or a sales pitch can list dozens of choices, and sorting each into owning or lending shows what it can do for you and how it can lose your money.

As an owner, your money rises and falls with what you own, so there’s no cap on your gain, and you can lose everything you paid. As a lender, you’re owed interest and your money back, so your return is mostly that interest. You lose if the borrower can’t pay, and your money buys less over time if prices climb faster than your interest.

Funds don’t add a third group. A fund bundles many stocks, many loans, or both, so it does the job of what it holds and carries the same risks.

These make you an owner, and their main job is growth.

These make you a lender. Their job is income and safety, and their value usually swings less than ownership’s.

These are funds, which bundle many of the investments above, and holding many investments at once limits the damage when one fails.

A mutual fund and an exchange-traded fund (ETF) differ in how you buy and sell them, not in what they can hold.

Options and other derivatives, contracts tied to another investment’s price, fit neither group. An option is a contract that lets you buy or sell an investment at a set price by a set date. It’s a bet on where the price goes. A buyer loses everything paid if the option expires worthless, and a seller’s losses can be unlimited.

Naming the group and what makes it lose value matters most with a product you can’t place. Say you’re offered a note paying a “guaranteed” 9%. A note is a loan, a company’s written promise to pay you back, so it sits with the lenders. But if it’s a loan to one small company with no credit rating, you could lose all of it if that company fails, a risk more like owning a stock than lending to a bank. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) warns that notes like this, sold widely to individual investors, are often scams.

A loan’s interest rate is the quickest clue to its risk. When it pays far more than Treasuries or insured CDs of the same length, the extra interest is the borrower paying you to accept a bigger chance of losing your money.

Then match the group to the job and the timeline. Large-company stocks as a group have lost money in about one of every three years, on average, the SEC’s guide to asset allocation says, so ownership suits money you won’t touch for years. Money you’ll need within a few years belongs on the lending side, where savings, CDs, and Treasury bills rarely lose money.

Buy stocks, bonds, or funds for a goal through one of the best online brokers.

#8463. Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

“I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”

So, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!)

Among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore new places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

With all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

While my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the big-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.)

This level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

As we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

In summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a new cost too since I was self-insured back then.

My budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

This strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible plan ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze plan in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

But as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

When it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which says that,

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

For me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

The only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I currently live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out.  I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

But I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

In the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

But for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

Mr. Money Mustache January 17, 2025, 9:41 am

My boy is almost grown up now (turning nineteen this month!) but those expenses were indeed higher during certain parts of his childhood.

We never had mandatory childcare because both parents retired before he was born – specifically so we could both team up as stay at home parents. But we still paid for part time preschool to get him out in the world mingling with other kids, and it paid off in friendships for both him and for us to this day.

I think that it’s totally worth spending money on things that your kid wants to do. But drawing the line short of forcing them into being on multiple sports teams just because you think it would be food for them. And prioritizing local things so you’re not spending multiple hours in the car every week.

Kids benefit from lots of self-directed play time with their siblings and parents and friends in nature, and many organized activities take them directly away from this. So, a middle ground between the standard rich suburbanite lifestyle and the traditional village upbringing could be ideal.

It is a “subsidy” in the sense that it reduces monthly/yearly cash requirements by the amount of principal+interest (and in the case of MMM, insurance since he chooses to self-insure). If you have a mortgage then you have a requirement to pay the mortgage every month (PITI), but in MMM’s case he only pays the ‘T’ part or taxes.

If he had a mortgage, then his $30k/year spend would probably be closer to $60k/year (or something, depending on the amount financed, interest rates, insurance, etc.). #8461. Weekend Warm-Up: Sending Ivindo Falls

Gabon Uncharted: Sending Ivindo Falls follows a crew of young kayakers, as they attempt to paddle 150km down the Ivindo River’s many rapids, gorges, and waterfalls.

The four kayakers are what the film’s narrator calls the “top of the crop.” After taking a moment to admire this charming malaphor (I think our narrator has combined “cream of the crop” and “top of the class”) we meet the Send team. Leader Adrian Mattern of Germany spent years planning their trip to Gabon, bringing with him the talkative Dane Jackson, patient Kalob Grady, and Bren Orton. Orton signed on with the shiny-faced, inevitably short-lived optimism of a youngster in 1914 headed for the front, sure of being home by Christmas.

“Apparently,” the narrator notes, “no one told him what he was getting into on this trip.”

Once on the ground, they load up their supplies and set out on a long stretch of flat water. Struggling along behind, we meet the film crew, an interesting behind-the-scenes look at the process of filming a professional, well-funded adventure documentary. Filmmaker Olaf Obsommer, photographer David Sodomka, and narrator David Arnaud do everything the Send team does, backward and in heels. Or, no — I’m thinking of Ginger Rogers.

Obsommer was part of the first team to scout the river by kayak in 2007. They portaged past most of the rapids for safety. Nowadays, better kayaks and the ability to scout ahead by drone will, hopefully, let them complete what he started.

At the first of four whitewater sections, Kongou, they settle in to take the rocky labyrinth piece by piece. If they take the wrong branch, they’ll be heading over a 25m waterfall.

Adrian is entranced by Kongou Falls, and only when the team delicately sit him down and explain that he would very likely drown, which would be awkward, does he agree to move on. Photo: Screenshot

They work their way down the river looking for rapids that will not kill them immediately. On the way, they get advice from Juste Parfait Zangonga, a local expert, on how to not be killed by elephants, gorillas, crocodiles, vipers, or hippos.

The next rapids, Mingouli, are less maze, more rollercoaster. The Send team can finally start living up to their name. Between first descents, they paddle past a family of elephants and get devoured by insects.

First descent down a tricky section of Mingouli. Photo: Screenshot

Kouata Mango, section three, is where Mattern finally gets to send a massive waterfall. The team agrees that this one is less likely to kill him badly, and over the side he goes.

Tsengue Lelendi, the final set of rapids, rounds out the trip. The laconic Kaleb takes a look at one particularly rough section and tells our narrator that the rapid is unrunnable. The rest of the team spends a long time debating it, anyway. Lo and behold, he’s right. After scouting with drones, mapping every angle, and discussing the route at length, they agree to skip a section of the rapid. The chain will still have just a few missing links left.

“A part of this river will remain untouched,” Arnaud concludes, “as it should, probably.”

Red Bull doesn’t allow embeds, but you can watch the full film here.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8460. How the Stock Market Works – Own All of It Instead of Trading

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

The stock market is a network of exchanges and trading firms where your broker gets your orders filled, usually by a professional on the other side. Don’t try to out-trade them. Use a brokerage account or your 401(k) to buy a fund that owns the whole stock market, and hold it for years.

When a newscast says the market rose 1%, it usually means an index such as the S&P 500, a single number that tracks a set of stocks, rose 1% that day. The number moves as investors change their expectations for companies’ future profits.

Every move in that number comes from trades between buyers and sellers. You place an order with a broker, the company that holds your investment account. The broker sends it to an exchange such as the New York Stock Exchange or Nasdaq, or to a market maker, a firm that will buy or sell a stock at prices it posts publicly. A stock listed on one exchange can trade on another or with a market maker, so where it’s listed barely matters to you.

Whoever takes the other side of your order is usually a professional. In 2022, the Securities and Exchange Commission said brokers sent more than 90% of individual investors’ orders to trade right away to a small group of off-exchange trading firms. Those firms typically fill the orders themselves. Trying to out-trade them rarely pays. When economists Brad Barber and Terrance Odean studied 66,465 households at one large brokerage firm from 1991 to 1996, those who traded most earned 11.4% a year, while the market returned 17.9%.

So skip the trading and own the whole market for years. Profits, interest rates, and the economy drive stock prices over the long run, while fear and greed swing them day to day. Open a brokerage account or use a 401(k), the retirement plan many employers offer. In either one, buy a total stock market index fund, which tracks an index of the entire U.S. stock market. In a 401(k) without one, pick the broadest stock index fund the plan offers.

Then set up automatic purchases of a fixed amount every payday, and leave the fund alone through the market’s drops.

Compare the best online brokers for beginners to choose where to open the account.

#8459. Dhaulagiri: Rope Fixing Halted For Unclear Reasons

About 20 climbers from several teams had planned to start their summit push on Dhaulagiri today, and conditions couldn’t be better: bluebird skies, low wind, and setting snow. So why are climbers stuck at Camp 2? And why are they so angry?

“We are…stuck here at Camp 2 waiting for the route above us to be fixed,” Paul Clarke of Australia texted to ExplorersWeb this morning.

As Clarke explained, the Sherpa team from Seven Summit Treks assigned to fix the route on Dhaulagiri this year refuses to lay ropes on the last sections above Camp 3.

“From what we are being told here at Camp 2, SST’s VVIP clients are no longer planning to climb higher,” Clarke said. “As a result, the company has little motivation to continue fixing the route for the remaining climbers.

The rope-fixing team had laid ropes until some 400m above Camp 3 earlier last week. The SST leader, Makalu Sherpa, shared his latest update on Friday. At that time, he reported everything was going well. The rope-fixing team made good progress while the clients waited at Camp 2. Neither SST nor 14 Peaks Expeditions has updated about Dhaulagiri since then. There have been no safety concerns reported during the current push.

In recent years, 8,000m peaks have been fixed either by a dedicated team assigned by the Expedition Operators Association of Nepal or by agreement among the companies on the mountain. They assign the rope fixing to a team of volunteers, whom the other operators all chip in to pay. Most 8,000m clients these days lack the skills to climb on their own and depend entirely on fixed ropes (and a packed trail) prepared by Sherpas.

The assigned rope-fixing team may stop for safety reasons, such as bad weather or risky conditions. We are waiting for further statements to clarify the situation. For now, unless a different group of Sherpas takes over, there will be no summit push.

This has frustrated those like Clarke and his climbing partner, Xenia Santha of Hungary. The pair patiently remained at Base Camp during the storm two weeks ago and have been at Camp 2 for five days, waiting for their moment. It’s mid-October, and there will probably be no further opportunities for them.

Today, Anni Penttila of Finland posted a text in Finnish on Instagram that translates to:

“Nothing came of it this time, either. It’s so disappointing that there’s really nothing to say at this point. Everyone turned back to Base Camp today.”

Anni Penttila’s story today from Dhaulagiri.

As the clients all retreat, Andrzej Bargiel remains at Base Camp with his large support and film team. The Polish skier intends to climb and ski down Dhaulagiri without oxygen. He has already skied eight other 8,000m peaks in that style, including Everest.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That said, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like new credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most important issues for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

One step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

While secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

In fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

There are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an issue with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

World-class Japanese hospitality at a fraction of the cash price via partner bookings

Picture this: you're settled into your own private suite at 37,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific. The door closes. A flight attendant in a crisp JAL uniform offers you a warm towel and asks how you'd like your appetizer served. The flat bed is already made with a proper duvet. Outside the window, the sun is setting over the ocean. You're nine hours into a 12-hour flight to Tokyo, and you feel more rested than you did when you boarded. This is JAL's Sky Suite — one of the most celebrated business class products in the world — and with the right travel rewards strategy, your family can experience it for a fraction of what everyone else is paying. Here's the math that stops people cold: a round-trip business class ticket from San Francisco to Tokyo on JAL typically retails for **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's not a typo. Premium transcontinental fares are genuinely that expensive, and most people simply accept that they'll never sit up front on a 12-hour flight across the Pacific. But the ChooseFI community knows better. That same seat — the same flat bed, the same Champagne, the same Sky Suite cocoon — is available for **60,000 miles** when booked through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. At a retail value of $5,000 to $10,000, you're looking at **8.3 to 16.7 cents per point** in value. For context, most travel rewards experts consider anything above 1.5 cents per point a good redemption. This one can be up to *eleven times* that benchmark. The pricing inefficiency exists because partner award programs — like Alaska and American — use fixed award charts that were negotiated years ago, before JAL's hard product became one of the most sought-after cabins in the sky. JAL hasn't raised these partner pricing levels proportionally as cash fares have climbed. The gap between what you pay in points and what the market charges in dollars is enormous, and it's yours to exploit right now. This isn't a loophole that's about to close tomorrow. It's a structural feature of the loyalty system — one that rewards people who understand how to use their points strategically rather than burning them on domestic economy upgrades. For anyone on the path to financial independence, where every dollar and every point is treated with intention, this is exactly the kind of asymmetric opportunity worth understanding.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: JAL's own frequent flyer program is not where you want to book this award. This is the aha moment that separates casual points users from strategic ones.

JAL operates its own loyalty program — JAL Mileage Bank — but it charges significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often running $100 to $500 or more per ticket. When you book JAL business class through JAL Mileage Bank itself, those surcharges erode a substantial portion of your points value before you even leave the ground. The ChooseFI community's editorial guidance here is unambiguous: book JAL through partner programs to avoid this tax on your redemption.

There are two primary programs where you can book JAL business class at 60,000 miles round-trip on the transpacific route:

Alaska Mileage Plan prices JAL business class at 60,000 miles for a round-trip between North America and Japan. Alaska is a oneworld partner of JAL and honors JAL's genuinely strong award availability. Critically, Alaska does not pass through JAL's fuel surcharges to awards booked through Mileage Plan. This is a massive advantage.

American AAdvantage also prices the same route at 60,000 miles round-trip. Both programs use fixed award charts, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash fares do — a $10,000 ticket at peak cherry blossom season costs exactly the same points as a ticket in a slower travel month.

Neither Alaska Mileage Plan nor American AAdvantage is a direct transfer partner from the major US bank programs in the same way Chase or Amex partners work. However, you have real pathways:

For Alaska and American miles specifically, the strongest earning strategies involve:

Both Alaska and American use fixed award charts — meaning the price in miles is the same regardless of how high the cash price climbs. This is the structural inefficiency at work. A seat that retails for $10,000 during peak season still costs 60,000 miles. The chart doesn't care about demand; it just prices by region and cabin. As long as JAL releases availability — and they do — the gap between cash cost and points cost remains enormous.

JAL also allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award, which means you can potentially add a stop in Tokyo itself while continuing to another Japanese city, or fly into one city and out of another — all at no additional miles cost.

This is the cardinal rule of all travel rewards bookings: never transfer points until you have confirmed availability. Points transfers are generally irreversible.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) to search for JAL award availability. Because BA is also a oneworld partner, their search tool shows you JAL award space. Search for your route (e.g., SFO to NRT) in business class. Any availability you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well. Look for "J" class availability, which represents business class award space.

You can also call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522 or American Airlines at 1-800-433-7300 and ask their agents to search JAL availability on your dates. Agents sometimes see space that doesn't show up online.

JAL's booking window opens 360 days in advance. For peak travel periods — Golden Week in Japan (late April to early May), cherry blossom season (late March to early April), and the summer holidays — availability disappears fast. Set a calendar reminder to search and book as soon as the window opens for your target dates.

For travel year-round outside those peaks, JAL is known for releasing strong business class availability, which is why this sweet spot earns a 4/5 on availability. You have real flexibility here.

Decide whether you'll book through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. Both charge 60,000 miles round-trip. The key differentiator: Alaska does not pass through fuel surcharges. If minimizing out-of-pocket costs is your priority, Alaska is the better choice.

For Alaska miles: Apply for the Bank of America Alaska Airlines Visa, earn the welcome bonus, and use shopping portals and partner promotions to top up. For American miles: The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select or Barclays AAdvantage Aviator cards offer solid welcome bonuses. You'll need a minimum of 60,000 miles per person.

If you need to use the Capital One → JAL Mileage Bank transfer path, initiate the transfer from your Capital One portal. Transfers post in 1-2 days. Note that booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly will incur fuel surcharges.

For Alaska: Call 1-800-252-7522 or book online at alaskaair.com/partner-awards. Online booking of JAL awards through Alaska can be hit-or-miss; calling is often more reliable.

For American: Book at aa.com or call. American's website allows partner award searches, though calling often surfaces additional availability.

Once booked, confirm your ticket number, that the cabin shows as "Business" (not an upgrade), and request your preferred meal. JAL offers Western and Japanese meal options — request ahead. Your seat assignment on the 787-9 Sky Suite or 777-300ER Apex Suite can be made at booking.

The core arbitrage here is the difference between booking through JAL's own program versus booking through oneworld partner programs. JAL Mileage Bank imposes significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets — often $100 to $500 per ticket — which erodes the points value substantially. But Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage can book the exact same JAL-operated flights with zero fuel surcharges because they use their own award charts and pricing rules. You are flying on JAL's aircraft with JAL's crew and JAL's business class product, but paying through a partner program's more favorable pricing. This is the same structural mismatch that creates sweet spots throughout the oneworld alliance — the booking program's pricing does not match the operating airline's product quality.

Let's run the numbers on a specific scenario that thousands of ChooseFI members have used as a benchmark: San Francisco (SFO) to Tokyo Narita (NRT) in JAL business class, round-trip for two people.

A quick search on Google Flights or JAL's own website for this route in business class will typically show cash prices ranging from $5,000 to $10,000 per person — let's use $7,000 as a reasonable midpoint for this example. For two people, you're looking at a $14,000 cash outlay before you even think about hotels in Tokyo.

Booked through Alaska Mileage Plan: 60,000 Alaska miles per person, round-trip. For two travelers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles total, plus taxes and fees (which Alaska keeps minimal for JAL awards, typically under $100 for the pair).

The CPP math: $7,000 in value ÷ 60,000 miles = 11.7 cents per point — squarely in the middle of the 8.3-to-16.7-cent range and nearly 8 times what most people get burning points on domestic economy tickets.

On the 777-300ER, you may get the Apex Suite — a staggered configuration with direct aisle access from every seat and a similarly flat, private sleeping environment.

Beyond the hardware: JAL's service is routinely ranked among the best in the world. The meal service for a 12-hour transpacific flight is multi-course, the sake selection is curated, and the attention to detail in Japanese hospitality culture elevates the experience above what the points price alone suggests.

You'll also access the JAL First Class Lounge or JAL Business Class Lounge at Narita on the return — another perk included with your business class boarding pass. By the time you land in San Francisco after a flat-bed sleep and a proper breakfast service, you've experienced what most travelers save for a once-in-a-lifetime trip. With travel rewards, it can be your default way to cross the Pacific.

British Airways' award search at ba.com is one of the best tools for seeing oneworld partner availability without committing any miles. Use it to scout JAL space across multiple dates before you transfer a single point. It shows business class availability clearly and quickly.

JAL's award calendar opens 360 days in advance. For anyone targeting cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or Golden Week (late April to early May), you should be searching and booking at the 360-day mark, not 60 days out. These are the hardest windows to find availability. Outside peak Japan travel seasons, this is much more forgiving.

JAL Mileage Bank allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award. If you're booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly (accepting the fuel surcharges), you can fly into Tokyo and out of Osaka, for example, without additional miles. This is a genuine value-add for anyone planning a broader Japan itinerary — no backtracking required.

This is a small thing that makes a big difference. Request the Japanese meal option when booking. It's more authentic, better-suited to the overall experience, and — in the ChooseFI spirit of intentionality — it's why you chose this airline over a generic carrier.

This is the single most common and most painful mistake. Points transfers are almost always one-way and irreversible. Never, under any circumstances, transfer points to a program before you have verbal or written confirmation of the award space you intend to book.

As emphasized in the program overview: JAL charges significant fuel surcharges on awards booked through its own program — $100 to $500 or more. For transpacific routes, always book through Alaska or American to avoid these fees. The data is explicit on this point.

If you do earn JAL Mileage Bank miles directly, note that they expire 36 months from the date earned on a rolling basis. If you let a balance sit idle, you may lose miles before you've accumulated enough to book. Keep the balance active through small purchases or partner activity.

This sweet spot is best suited for couples and individual travelers who are targeting Japan specifically — whether it's a bucket-list trip, a first visit to Tokyo, or a multi-city Japan itinerary. The fixed 60,000-mile price per person means that families with young children will need to accumulate significant balances (60,000 miles per ticketed passenger), which pushes the complexity and earning requirement higher.

You need a minimum of 60,000 Alaska miles or 60,000 American AAdvantage miles per person to execute this redemption. For a couple, that's 120,000 miles — achievable with two well-chosen credit card welcome bonuses plus some additional earning through everyday spending or partner promotions.

This redemption is not ideal for beginners — it scores 2/5 on beginner-friendliness, and honestly, that's accurate. The booking path involves navigating partner award searches, understanding the difference between booking programs (Alaska vs. JAL Mileage Bank) and why it matters for surcharges, and potentially calling airlines rather than booking online. If you're on your first or second travel rewards card and still building your foundational understanding, this is one to put on a future list while you sharpen your skills.

For the FI-focused traveler who has been in the travel rewards ecosystem for a year or more, this is a landmark redemption. The CPP ceiling of 16.7 cents per point represents one of the highest-value uses of any points in a North American loyalty portfolio. If you believe in maximizing every dollar you earn and every point you accumulate — and the ChooseFI community does — this is the kind of redemption that justifies the entire system.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty**, and that rating is honest. It's not the most complex thing in the travel rewards world, but it has enough moving parts that going in without preparation can lead to frustration or costly mistakes. **What specifically makes it moderate:** First, the **earning path is not plug-and-play**. Unlike Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, which transfer to dozens of partners instantly, Alaska miles and American miles are earned primarily through co-branded credit cards and flying. There's no one magic transferable currency that flows directly into these programs at full value. Second, **the booking process often requires a phone call**. Online partner award booking through Alaska and American works inconsistently. Many experienced travelers report that calling the airline's award desk surfaces availability that the website doesn't show — which is a normal part of the process but adds friction. Third, **fuel surcharge awareness matters**. Understanding *why* you book through Alaska or American instead of JAL Mileage Bank directly is a non-obvious nuance that could cost you real money if you don't get it right. **Three tips to overcome the challenge:** 1. **Use BA.com as your availability scouting tool** — it gives you a clean, visual look at JAL award space without committing any miles. 2. **Call Alaska or American directly** when online searches fail. Agents are well-versed in partner award booking and can often find and hold space while you confirm your miles balance. 3. **Build your miles balance before you start searching.** Having 70,000+ miles in hand (a small buffer above 60,000) before you begin reduces stress and gives you flexibility on dates. If you've already completed one or two simpler travel rewards bookings and understand the basics of award searches, this is well within reach. The effort is real — and the payoff is a flat bed over the Pacific.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) and search for your route in business class. Because BA is a oneworld partner, their search tool shows JAL award space. Search across multiple dates to find availability. Any space you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well.

Both charge 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges. Alaska miles can be earned through the Alaska Airlines Visa card or transferred from Marriott Bonvoy (3:1). AAdvantage miles can be earned through Citi cards or transferred from various hotel programs. Choose based on which miles you have or can earn most efficiently.

Only transfer points after confirming award availability on ba.com. For Alaska, earn through card spending or Marriott transfers. For AAdvantage, earn through Citi cards. Never transfer before confirming space — transfers are generally irreversible.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan or book on aa.com to ticket the JAL-operated flight. For Alaska, phone booking is required for partner awards. For AA, search on aa.com and book online if the JAL space appears. Confirm your JAL seat assignment on jal.com after ticketing.

JAL Mileage Bank imposes fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often adding $100 to $500 per ticket on transpacific routes. Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage book the exact same JAL-operated flights at the same 60,000-mile price but with zero fuel surcharges. You fly the same plane, same seat, same service — but pay significantly less out of pocket.

JAL opens its award calendar approximately 360 days in advance. For peak seasons like cherry blossom season (late March to early April) and Golden Week (late April to early May), you should begin searching the day the window opens. Off-peak dates are generally easier to find with 3 to 6 months of lead time.

However, BA charges fuel surcharges on partner awards, so this path is less favorable than Alaska or AA. The cleanest Chase path is to earn Alaska or AA miles through other means.

JAL business class via Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage is the definitive sweet spot for anyone targeting Japan. At 60,000 miles one-way with zero fuel surcharges, you are booking a $5,000 to $10,000 cash experience for a fraction of the cost through a partner program pricing arbitrage. The key is searching ba.com for availability before transferring a single point, booking 360 days out for peak cherry blossom or Golden Week dates, and choosing between Alaska and AA based on which miles you can earn most efficiently. JAL's business class product — lie-flat seats, exceptional cuisine, and Japanese hospitality — delivers an experience that justifies the points spend and then some. This is the redemption that puts Japan within reach for every FI-minded traveler.

#8455. Kyrgyz Climb 'Eternal Flame' Route on Nameless Tower

On September 28, a Kyrgyz team made its country’s first ascent of 6,239m Nameless Tower.

The expedition was led by Mikhail Mikhailov, known for his role in the 2004 North Face ascent of Jannu, which earned a Piolet d’Or, and for the 2009 first ascent of Peak 6134 on Minya Konka with Alexander Ruchkin, according to Mountain.ru.

Other members of the Nameless Tower group include Mikhail Danichkin, Timur Akbashev, Aidar Akbashev, Zarina Kutanova, and Aleksei Pototsky. The Kyrgyz team carried out the technical climb of this soaring granite spire, one of the Trango Towers, via the famous Eternal Flame route.

Nameless Tower. Photo: Timur Akbashev/Mountain.ru

Eternal Flame is one of the most celebrated big-wall routes in the Karakoram. It was first climbed in September 1989 by Kurt Albert, Wolfgang Gullich, Christof Stiegler, and Milan Sykora on Nameless Tower’s South Face. The original climbing route is roughly 650m long, on a vertical wall with a total height of about 1,000m. It was graded VI, 7b+, A2.

The route combines sustained hard granite climbing with the altitude, logistics, and objective hazards of a 6,000m Karakoram peak, which is why it has remained a major objective for both free climbers and traditional alpinists. The Kyrgyz ascent adds its country’s name to the short list of teams that have summited by this classic line.

Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

Your deposits would total just $10,800 over those 30 years, so the other $26,000 or so is investment growth, more than twice what you put in.

The Securities and Exchange Commission’s compound interest calculator at Investor.gov runs the same math for three daily amounts, at a hypothetical 7% return a year, with growth added monthly:

At $1 a day, the third decade adds about $21,000, more than the $16,000 built in the first two, which is why starting at 25 instead of 35 matters so much. Actual returns change from year to year, and some years lose money, so treat these figures as illustrations, not promises.

Make the deposit automatic, weekly or monthly, so it happens whether or not you remember. A $7 weekly deposit does the same job as $30 a month. Choose an investing app with no monthly fee, since a $3 monthly charge would cost 10% of each $30 deposit.

#8453. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Adventure Has No Retirement Age: Adventure is continuing well into the ninth decade of life for a growing number of paddlers and hikers. Ninety-one-year-old Dale “Greybeard” Sanders only took up extreme endurance challenges at 80. Since then, he has paddled the Mississippi River from source to sea twice, completed the Missouri River Race, and this year reclaimed the record as the oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail.

The challenge of competing and breaking records keeps him going, but not everyone is chasing endurance records. For Wendy Eden, 77, the goal is just to be out in nature and to keep exploring her beloved Canadian wilderness on her own. That means adapting her approach as she gets older.

I Hitchhiked From Sydney to Perth: Aston Brown describes his experience of hitchhiking across Australia from Sydney to Perth. He sees hitchhiking as an opportunity to surrender control and connect with people he would otherwise never meet.

Far more common in the 1970s and 1980s, the practice plummeted in Australia because of its association with serial killer Ivan Milat, who targeted hitchhikers. Now it is starting to pick up again, as online communities and social media introduce it to a new generation.

Brown recognizes that hitchhiking carries dangers and that his experience as a man does not reflect the risks women traveling alone face. Yet his journey left him with a sense of connection. He spent three days and 1,900km traveling with Neil, a 79-year-old widower, on a four-month road trip around Australia. He also met a Zimbabwean family who had left the U.S. because of gun violence and immigration crackdowns, a retired tractor enthusiast, and Doug, head of Australia’s national science agency, who invited him birdwatching to see one of the country’s rarest birds.

She Had a Will To Live: A 72-year-old hiker survived six nights in the wilderness after falling 30m down a steep embankment. Mary Beth Granbery was on the Cabin Creek Trail near Mount Shasta in California when she fell.

She had set out on a multi-day camping trip and was expected home within four days. When she failed to return, friends and family raised the alarm. Rescuers found her camper van at the trailhead and launched a search. They found her one day later, at the bottom of the embankment. Despite suffering injuries from the fall, dehydration, and hypothermia from the cool nights, Granbery was still conscious when the rescue team reached her.

Across Madagascar To Find The World’s Last Lemurs: Geena Truman and her husband took a 2,500km road trip across Madagascar to search for lemurs. In a rented 4×4, they set off from Antananarivo. On the RN7 highway, they drove through rainforest, highland rice paddies, canyons, and desert, encountering rare species including golden bamboo lemurs, ring-tailed lemurs, and Verreaux’s sifakas.

Leaving the highway, they ended up on rough tracks with tricky river crossings, mud pits, and routes so difficult to navigate that they hired a local guide, known as a pisteur, to find their way.

Driving through Madagascar’s iconic baobab trees towards Tsingy de Bemaraha and Kirindy Reserve. Photo: Geena Truman

Grand Ole Roadtrip: In the summer of 1976, six young climbers piled into a blue Ford van and drove west to tackle Wyoming’s Teton Range. That first trip to the Tetons saw them face loose rock on the Enclosure Ice Couloir, a terrifying slide down the Skillet Couloir that nearly carried two of the group over a glacier’s edge, and two separate encounters with violent thunderstorms that left them clinging to exposed rock.

At the heart of all of this was the Grand Teton Climbers’ Ranch (GTRC), an affordable base for mountaineers. It offered more than a cheap bed: It was a place to meet climbing partners, exchange stories, and recover from the day over shared meals. Today, the GTRC remains one of their favorite places on Earth.

Renate Powell Completes Munro Round in Barefoot Shoes: Renate Powell has completed her second round of Scotland’s 282 Munros, this time in barefoot shoes. The keen hillwalker turned to minimalist footwear in her forties when an old skiing injury left her knee in constant pain.

She started by walking just 100m a day, then spent more than a year gradually building up to take on a Munro in her barefoot shoes. Fourteen years after first trying them, she continues her long-distance walking, without the knee replacement that was initially suggested.

Climbing the Cuillin Munro in barefoot shoes. Photo: Gillian Parker

Mad, Bad and Dangerous To Know: Sir Ranulph Fiennes, 82, has been living with Parkinson’s for seven years. He’s been out of the public eye for two years, and his current state is uncertain.

Fiennes spent much of his life building a remarkable expedition career after serving in the military. His 1979-82 Transglobe Expedition saw him and fellow former SAS soldiers Charles Burton and Oliver Shepard complete a 60,000km circumnavigation using surface travel, crossing both Poles.

He later completed a 2,170km unsupported ski crossing of Antarctica with Mike Stroud, and attempted to reach the North Pole unsupported five times. After severe frostbite during a 2000 expedition, he famously amputated his own dead fingertips with a fretsaw. This article plots out the timeline of his extraordinary expeditions.

A Climber Has Now Called For Help Three Times in 2026: Two climbers had to be rescued on September 22 after becoming stranded on the 500m White Dyke scramble on British Columbia’s Edge Peak. The pair set out at 8:30 am, but later that afternoon, with only three hours until sunset, the less experienced climber was too exhausted to continue.

After two hours attempting to rescue themselves, they activated a Garmin SOS beacon. This is the third time one of the climbers in the duo has had to be rescued this year. Rescue veteran Brent Boulet warned that social media seems to be drawing less experienced people onto technical routes. He stressed the importance of realistic timing, turning back when necessary, and knowing a climbing partner’s capabilities before setting out.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

You don’t need thousands of dollars to start investing. Big brokers have no account minimums, and fractional shares let $5 buy a slice of a fund that owns 500 leading U.S. companies. Open a brokerage account and invest what you can spare now, since a month spent saving up is a month that money isn’t invested.

Investing a few dollars at a time made little sense when each trade came with a fee. Until October 2019, Charles Schwab charged $4.95 for an online stock trade, almost all of a $5 purchase.

Schwab now charges no commission on online trades of U.S. stocks and ETFs, the exchange-traded funds that trade like stocks, and Fidelity doesn’t either. Start in a brokerage account or a Roth IRA, a retirement account whose withdrawals in retirement are tax-free under IRS rules. You need income from work to put money in a Roth IRA, and the IRS limits how much higher earners can add. A workplace 401(k) needs no lump sum at all, since it takes an amount you pick from each paycheck, and any employer match adds to it.

Put the first dollars into one broad index fund, a fund that tracks a market index such as the S&P 500, which includes 500 leading U.S. companies. Splitting a small account among a few single stocks makes all of it depend on how those companies do.

Once your starter emergency fund is in place, invest a set amount every week. At $25 a week, you put $1,300 a year into a Roth IRA without ever writing a big check. Each deposit buys more of the fund the week it arrives instead of waiting in checking.
