Do This: Set a Monthly Calendar Reminder for the 1st

Flying Blue Promo Rewards are time-sensitive by design. The best routes with the best dates are gone within 24–48 hours of announcement. Put a recurring reminder on your calendar. Treat the 1st of each month like a mini-event.

Do This: Keep a Points Buffer in Your Transferable Accounts

Because Promo Rewards require fast action and the best transfer partners (Chase, Amex, Citi) are instant, you want at least 40,000–80,000 points already sitting in your transferable account before the announcement. Don't be in a position where you need to wait on a credit card statement to close before you can transfer.

Do This: Use Open-Jaw Routing to Maximize Your Trip

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing. Book into Paris (CDG) and out of Amsterdam (AMS) — or any combination of Air France/KLM hub cities — and you've just built a multi-country European trip into a single award booking. This is the kind of routing flexibility that turns a one-city trip into a proper adventure.

Do This: Track Multiple Months of Route Patterns

Promo routes rotate monthly, but certain routes appear repeatedly — particularly transatlantic and routes between European hubs and Africa or the Middle East. After 2–3 months of observation, you'll start to recognize patterns and can plan your travel around routes that are likely to repeat.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability

This is the single biggest mistake beginners make. Always confirm the specific flight, date, and cabin availability before transferring points. Miles are a one-way street — you cannot transfer them back. If availability disappears after you've transferred, you're left with Flying Blue miles that may not be useful for your target route at standard (non-Promo) pricing.

Avoid This: Ignoring Standard Award Pricing

Flying Blue's dynamic pricing outside of Promo Rewards can be punishingly expensive. A Business class seat that costs 40,000 Promo miles might cost 90,000+ miles at standard dynamic pricing. Always wait for the Promo if you can — patience pays.

The ideal earning setup for this redemption combines a Chase Sapphire Reserve (3x on travel and dining, instant transfer to Flying Blue) with an Amex Gold or Platinum (4x on dining/groceries or 5x on flights respectively, also instant transfer). Between two cards, you can accumulate 40,000–80,000 points in a single year of normal household spending.

Best For: Flexible Couples and Solo Travelers Who Plan in Advance

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI community member who thinks in systems, not spontaneous splurges. You're someone who has already built a transferable points balance of at least 40,000–80,000 points across Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, or Citi ThankYou — and who can act decisively when the right route appears.

Couples are the sweet spot. Two people, two Business class seats, one incredible transatlantic experience. Solo travelers benefit enormously too — a single seat at 40,000 miles is one of the highest-CPP solo redemptions in the entire transferable points ecosystem.

Minimum Viable Setup: 40,000 Flying Blue miles or 40,000 transferable points in Chase, Amex, or Citi. A Flying Blue account with verified transfer links. The flexibility to travel within a 30-day window of whatever routes appear that month.

**Difficulty Rating: Hard — But for Specific, Solvable Reasons** This isn't hard because the booking process itself is complicated. Flyingblue.com is a functional, English-language booking tool that anyone can navigate. It's hard because of **timing and availability** — two factors that reward the prepared and punish the passive. **What Specifically Makes This Hard:** 1. **Monthly availability windows are brief.** You have 24–48 hours from the Promo announcement to act before the best dates disappear. If you're not watching, you miss the cycle entirely and wait another month. 2. **Dynamic pricing outside of Promo is punishing.** If you miss the Promo window and try to book a standard award on the same route, you could pay 2–3x more miles. The program's value is almost entirely concentrated in the monthly Promo structure. 3. **Coordination across accounts takes discipline.** Keeping 40,000–80,000 points liquid in a transferable account, not spending them on something else, and being ready to move instantly requires real points discipline. **Three Tips to Overcome the Challenge:** - **Automate your awareness.** Sign up for Flying Blue emails and follow deal-tracking communities so the announcement comes to you. - **Keep your points liquid in Chase or Amex.** The instant transfer speeds are your competitive advantage over slower-moving transfer paths. - **Be route-flexible, not date-flexible.** You may not get Paris in July, but you might get Amsterdam in September — and that's still an extraordinary redemption. If you're willing to build the habit of checking on the 1st of each month and keeping a points buffer ready, the hard part becomes routine. The ChooseFI community has proven this works — repeatedly.

Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com and enable email notifications. Keep at least 40,000 to 80,000 transferable points in your Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, or Bilt account. Set a recurring calendar reminder for the 1st of each month.

Visit flyingblue.com on the morning of the 1st (or within the first few days) to see the new Promo Rewards routes. Scan for destinations that match your interests. Note the discounted mile pricing and travel date windows — promos typically cover travel within the next 2 to 3 months.

Use the Flying Blue award search to check specific dates on the promo routes in business class. Confirm that seats are available at the promo price before you transfer any points. The calendar view lets you scan across multiple dates quickly.

Transfer the required miles from Chase (instant), Amex (1-2 days), Citi (instant), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Book on flyingblue.com the moment your miles arrive. Do not wait — promo availability is limited and the best dates disappear within hours.

Promo Rewards typically offer 25 to 50 percent off standard dynamic pricing. A business class transatlantic award that normally costs 80,000 to 100,000 miles one-way can drop to 40,000 to 50,000 miles on a Promo Reward. Additionally, fuel surcharges are eliminated on promo awards, saving another $100 to $300 per ticket that would otherwise be charged on standard awards.

Chase Ultimate Rewards and Citi ThankYou are the best because they transfer instantly to Flying Blue at a 1:1 ratio. Amex Membership Rewards and Capital One both transfer at 1:1 but take 1 to 2 business days. Bilt also transfers at 1:1. Since promo availability is time-sensitive, instant transfer partners give you a meaningful speed advantage.

Yes. Promo Rewards rotate destinations each month and cover specific travel date windows, typically 2 to 3 months out. You cannot choose which routes are discounted. The strategy works best for travelers who have a list of destinations they want to visit and can match those against whatever promos appear each month rather than needing a specific route on a specific date.

The best routes with the best dates typically sell out within 24 to 48 hours of the monthly announcement. Business class availability is particularly limited. Set a reminder for the 1st of each month and check within the first few hours of the announcement for the widest selection of dates and routes.

Flying Blue Promo Rewards is the most repeatable sweet spot in travel rewards because it renews every single month. While other sweet spots are one-time plays or annual opportunities, Promo Rewards gives you 12 chances per year to book premium cabin flights at 25 to 50 percent off standard pricing with no fuel surcharges. The system rewards exactly the kind of behavior the FI community already excels at: preparation, patience, and decisive action when the numbers align. Keep 40,000 to 80,000 transferable points in reserve, check on the 1st of every month, and book the moment you find a route that matches your travel list. Over time, this single strategy can deliver thousands of dollars in business class experiences at economy-level points costs.

#8438. Fractional Shares Let You Invest by the Dollar – but Switching Brokers Sells Them

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

With fractional shares, every dollar of a small deposit is invested at once instead of waiting in cash for a whole share. Set up automatic monthly buys of one broad index fund at a fractional-share broker, and expect the fractions to be sold, not transferred, if you switch brokers.

At $50 a month, buying only whole shares means a year of saving before you own one share of a $600 exchange-traded fund (ETF), a fund that trades like a stock. Fractions let each $50 buy about 0.083 of a share right away.

Which stocks and ETFs you can buy in fractions depends on the broker. Fidelity sells fractions of most stocks and ETFs listed on the NYSE or Nasdaq, from $1. J.P. Morgan Self-Directed Investing limits them to stocks in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 indexes and the ETFs on its eligible list, from $5. Vanguard sells them on its own ETFs, from $1.

The catch that costs money comes when you move your account. FINRA, the regulator that oversees brokers, says fractional shares can’t transfer to another firm, so only your whole shares move and the fractions are sold for cash. In a regular brokerage account, unlike an IRA, that sale can mean tax on any gain.

Fractions have smaller drawbacks too. Fidelity gives them no shareholder vote, and fractional orders often go through only during regular market hours. Some brokers also collect a day’s fractional orders from all their customers and send them to the market together, which can change the price you pay. None of that hurts the best use of fractions, which is automatic dollar-amount buys of one broad index ETF you hold for years.

Your fractions add up to whole shares as you keep buying, so moving your account never sells more than one share’s worth of each fund you hold.

To find a broker that sells fractions of the ETF you want, compare the best brokers for fractional share investing.

#8436. How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

Quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well. Back in February 2025, the market put the perfect cap on a multi year climb before stepping onto the wild roller coaster we’re currently riding. Since then it has seen some of the steepest drops and recoveries in history, losing a full 20% of its value at the bottom while somehow managing to end up right back near the peak as I’m writing this.

And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.

As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.

As I write this, we still don’t know the outcome of the worldwide tariff and trade battle that our unpredictable government has unleashed upon the world. But we’re already seeing the results: businesses are bracing for massive changes, currencies and interest rates are reacting, and regular investors like you and me are wondering what the future holds for our early retirement funds. Surveying my own group of friends, the reactions span the whole range of emotions from “this is a giant Nothingburger” to “we’re all totally screwed.”

So what’s the real answer? To get closer to that, we should start with the most basic question of:

A tariff is just a sales tax charged by our government on goods which are imported into the country.  They are paid by whoever is doing the importing – meaning you if you order something like an e-bike directly from a company in China, or by companies like Amazon, Walmart, or Apple which import products from other countries by the shipload.

But in the end, the tariffs aren’t paid by China or Amazon or Apple. They are paid by you, the end consumer, because if their cost of goods increases, a retailer is of course going to raise their prices to continue to make a profit.

Tariffs also affect companies directly: if Home Depot wants to build a new store or Chevron needs a new oil rig, the tariffs on imported steel, copper, lumber and a million other components will raise the cost of these construction projects. And they raise the cost of housing, because most of the building materials in houses come from multiple countries as well.

On average, tariffs will result in higher prices for everything just like any other broad-based sales tax. And just like most other taxes, the overall effect is to slow the economy and reduce our spending power. On the positive side, all that tax money flows into the government’s pocket which could help fund the national budget and even reduce the deficit.

Of course, every government needs at least some tax revenue to function, so it makes sense to use some mix of sales, income and corporate taxes to get there. The most important part is that the levels need to be as low as possible while still keeping the country running well, and as fair and predictable as possible, so that people and businesses have an incentive to work hard and the ability to plan far into the future.

And that’s where our current tariff regime gets it completely backwards. Donald Trump is throwing around random, extremely high tariff numbers as threats, then walking them back and changing them on an almost daily basis..

Whoa, that Sounds Mostly Bad – Is There a Good Side of Tariffs?

Sometimes, a country will use tariffs to protect their own domestic industries. For example, if you put a tax on imported Hondas, then General Motors cars will gain a competitive advantage – so GM will make more money. In this example, most consumers end up losing due to increased prices and decreased selection. But at least domestic auto manufacturers and their employees are happy.

This can be strategic (for example we might want to slap a tax on imported fighter jets to make sure Boeing and Lockheed can remain in business, for national defense purposes.) Or it can be corrupt (a politician might receive funding from kingpins in the steel industry, and in return then push through tariffs on imported steel to protect the profits of US steelmakers.)

And this isn’t just a Trump or Republican thing either – Joe Biden used tariffs during his terms in an attempt to please swing-state voters. One of the worst examples was a tax on imported solar panel components (which Trump has since raised even further, proving that Boneheadedness can be Bipartisan). These are sheets of cheap glass that literally pump the cheapest energy and easiest wealth into your country for 30 years as soon as you plug them in. Cheap energy lowers everyone’s cost of living while also boosting industry. There is no good reason to block such wealth from flowing across your borders.

Let’s go back to that hypothetical tax on Hondas, and let’s say it’s a big one like $5000. At that level, many buyers will start heading over to the GM dealer next door to consider what he’s selling. Sure, the GM cars may not be as good, but for five grand some people are going to settle in order to save some money.

Because of this, GM’s sales go up. So they hire more employees and build more factories. They might even develop some new models and new technologies in response to all that new demand. More people learn advanced skills and in the best case it becomes a virtuous circle.

But in exchange for this boom in the auto industry, everyone else has to pay more for slightly shittier cars and trucks. Higher vehicle prices means Amazon will have to spend more on their delivery fleet, so they will raise prices slightly on everything they sell. Somewhere a startup company or a medical breakthrough will be just a bit less likely to happen, because they are operating in an environment that is just a bit more expensive and a bit less efficient.

On top of that, with GM liberated from the hassle of competing with Honda, it will have less incentive to innovate and streamline itself. So its overall trajectory will be slower and less efficient even if its profits are higher.

This big picture effect is why most economists agree that tariffs should be used very sparingly. They almost always cause unexpected damage, decrease overall employment and slow down an economy, but sometimes (like for food security or national defense) those costs are worth paying.

So Why is Donald Trump Throwing Around Tariffs Like They Are The Best Thing Ever?

This has been confusing to almost everyone. If you take him at his word, he appears to have a Bizarro Opposite Universe belief system about economics. Donald has claimed in speeches that the tariffs will somehow make us wealthier. He’s focusing on the first-order effects like GM hiring more workers, while completely ignoring the fact that everything else in the country gets less efficient in exchange.

But when he announces larger tariffs, share prices go down, because everyone who actually runs or invests in US companies knows that of course they will make less money on average. When tariffs are paused or reduced, share prices go back up. Yet he keeps wielding the threats and we go back and forth.

It seems to be obvious to everyone except Donald himself that Tariffs are just a national sales tax rather than some clever sneaky strategic weapon, which leads to various theories that okay, maybe he knows that too but is just pretending in order to gain some influence.

So right now our entire economy is subject to the whims of a single person.. And as long as this is the case, we’re just the same as any other dictatorship – something our constitution was supposed to prevent with the whole “three independent branches of government” thing.

But presidents have tried to break out of their constitutional cage and get more power many times in the past, and this is just the latest example. The real test will be if our system eventually manages to stop this abuse and put itself back in balance as it always has in the past. You can already see this fight beginning to play out in our court system, in this Economist article:

Even without the 145% nonsense numbers that were thrown around a few months ago, they are still far higher than they have been in the last 75 years or more. While it would be hard to pin down the current numbers in a stationary blog post like this one, the key thing to remember is that our current US economy is built around very low tariffs and relatively free trade.

Why haven’t I noticed Prices Going Up Yet?

While the US economy is fueled by a constant stream of cargo ships, as a whole we function like the biggest cargo ship of all: we have a huge inventory and it takes a while to change directions.

So in normal times, we already have several months of inventory of most things in the country. And then when all this drama started, importers started placing even more orders to stockpile things in advance before the tariffs hit. And now that they are in place, we’re importing a lot less stuff.

For now, we’re still using up the stockpiled inventory, but imports have dropped significantly so we’re quickly running out of cheap goods. If that happens, we will probably start seeing shortages and price increases throughout this summer or fall. For some things like plastic party trinkets, we can do just fine without. But if we lose access to core useful things like tools and machinery, the economic consequences will be much less fun.

The most important phrase to remember in US politics and economics is the phrase “This too shall pass.” The only mystery right now is that we don’t know exactly how it will pass. So we could sketch out a few scenarios:

1) The current crazy-high tariffs really do stick around:

I personally think this is the less likely scenario because nobody really wants it. But just as a thought experiment, it might go something like this:

2) They do end up being just a negotiating tactic and we go back to mostly low tariffs.

In other words, the best way to win the tariff game is not to play it.

Just as much of US prosperity is built upon our huge population of 330 million people living in 50 states with open borders and no trade restrictions, all (friendly) countries of the world can benefit from the free exchange of goods, services and even people. We’re all human beings and if we treat each other with a collaborative respect, we all grow richer.

I started writing this article on April 2nd, when Donald announced his “Liberation Day” and the stock market reacted with the biggest drop since 1932. Some people panicked and locked in big losses despite decades of warnings from your favorite financial bloggers, like this unfortunate soul in the comments to a JL Collins post:

But as I watched over the next two months, we have bounced our way back up – with each drop in proposed tariffs triggering a corresponding increase in stock prices (a measure of investor enthusiasm of how bright our future looks).

Right now, the US stock market is just about back to its all-time high. This doesn’t match with our current level of tariffs, which are still about seven times higher than they were before the circus opened. But it shows that investors believe it’s all going to end with a truce and a resumption of free-ish international trade.

If they’re wrong, the roller coaster ride will still have some more fun in store for us. But as long as we eventually end our current experiment in “emergency” tariff dictatorship and get back to functioning as a democracy, things should be just fine in the long run. I’m still 100% invested myself, so that’s where I place my bet.

The Biggest Lesson: Don’t Form Your Opinions Based on News Headlines

Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us, with just a bit of sizzle and spice to pull in our attention. Unfortunately, nowadays the priorities have flipped where the primary goal is attention, and accuracy carries little or no weight. Even a totally inaccurate article makes money for the publisher.

So while Democrats and Republicans like to do battle over which media sources are biased, in reality they’re all wrong: all click-funded commercial media is biased – sometimes politically but even more importantly biased towards generating outrage and fear, because those generate more money.

1) Either ignore the media completely and focus on your own life, or

2) Become a subject matter expert on things you really care about, and then read the original sources whenever you want to learn about something.

I mostly practice option #1, but as a science and technology nerd I get into #2 in just the areas I find most interesting. And it’s amazing how the more deeply you understand a subject, the more you see just how wrong most media stories are about your area of expertise. Which means they’re probably pretty wrong about almost everything.

Great question – I tried to cover this in the article under the heading, “Why haven’t I noticed prices going up yet?”

First of all, most of the tariffs (or threatened tariffs) haven’t even hit yet.

But even when they do, the end result will be a bit unpredictable. Importers can of course shift supply to countries with lower tariffs or even domestic suppliers. Consumers will also react to rising prices by scaling back their spending, which shifts prices back down the supply/demand curve a little.

In the extreme case, high tariffs can even cause a recession which lowers demand for almost all goods and services, which means that prices for domestically produced services with elastic pricing might go down and bring the overall inflation numbers back in check. In other words, some people lose their jobs so on average there’s less money being spent on restaurants -> restaurants have to lower their prices.

Heck, in a good enough recession even house prices and rents will drop, which is the biggest factor in the inflation basket.

Might be semantic, but maybe tariffs are not “inflation”. It would be like saying that a VAT would be inflationary. Instead, this is a one-time step-function change in the cost of goods, then inflation (velocity) resumes on the new cost base. Oren Cass had an interesting blog article on this last week. At least food for thought – he posits that economists don’t actually think tariffs are inflationary.

100% the case. Inflation is caused by an increase in the money supply, by definition. It means your purchasing power is worth less. A one-time increase in a specific category of goods of 15% is not “inflation.” Meanwhile, every time the government uses printed (or digitally entered) dollars to spend trillions they don’t have, inflation grows massively and compounds, and for some reason, the majority of people don’t bat an eye.

A great analogy for inflation would be something like this… You are in charge of the county fair. There are a bunch of vendors of popcorn, cotton candy, and ride like ferris wheels, etc. You print tickets that visitors can use to acquire these goods and ride these rides, and the vendors set their own ticket prices. You and your friends discover you can give yourselves tickets and get more popcorn and ride more rides since you own the ticket machine. With the flood of tickets, the vendors realize they can (and need to) raise their prices. This is inflation. And it doesn’t matter if it’s due to your and your friends doing it for yourselves, or just doing it because of more guests coming to the fair (for “growth”).

I think the definition of inflation is a rise in prices not a rise in money supply. Money supply is one factor in that, but so is the overall supply and demand of everything that is for sale. Money supply is increased or decreased as needed in reaction to what’s happening with prices, in order to keep prices more stable, if the system is well managed.

In your county fair example, you are holding the number of vendors and the items and quantities for sale as a constant while increasing the number of tickets. In reality the fair’s mini-economy will grow and shrink over time, and if the ticket supply were forced to always stay constant the ticket prices of rides, popcorn and cotton candy would move up and down significantly in reaction.

“I think the definition of inflation is a rise in prices not a rise in money supply.”

Well, that’s the problem – that is wrong. A rise in prices is a symptom of inflation. It is not inflation nor is it the cause of inflation. Inflation is similar in concept to dilution.

No it’s not wrong. Inflation is prices going higher as time passes. The causes of inflation are debatable, but “inflation” is a word that refers to prices going up regardless of the cause.

It’s possible for money supply to increase without inflation. Japanese deflation and lost decades are a prime example.

One interesting note, on top of your spot on analysis of the impact of tariffs, is how hard economic data, as traditionally collected, is to interpret in 2025.

Specifically, the unemployment rate is really interesting to me.

Clearly, the prevailing sentiment is that it’s a tough market out there for most (but not all) employees. At BiggerPockets, we were getting TONS of applicants for every available job posting for months.

But, yet, the employment reports show low unemployment, and jobs added with each passing month. What gives?

I believe that the answer lies in the gig economy and with self-employed workers. There are some 50 million Americans working gig work, self-employed, or who work as contractors. Contrary to popular belief, there are many of this cohort who actively choose that lifestyle and prefer it over a full-time job, getting a better mixture of total income and flexibility.

However, when that work becomes harder and harder, and it is no longer feasible to support yourself or your family on your combined uber, amazon delivery, lyft, and doordash routine, you begin to take that unappealing job for $45K per year.

You are now worse off, in terms of total income and flexibility.

But the employment report shows it as a net positive.

I believe that this effect does two things:

1) Presents a false view of the economy as healthier than it actually is. 2) Gives the federal reserve free reign to be extra cautious about lowering rates – inflation is a bigger threat than the “jobs” report that they are mandated to watch.

That’s a really good point. Even outside of the business world, on a personal level it takes up mental energy.

Thank you for raising this point. The lack of concern about the impacts on businesses has been a real source of frustration for me.

My day job has given me a window into some industry sectors, including during Trump 1.0 and the trade war then. I always remember the small US steel manufacturer one of my colleagues spoke with at that time, when researching some of the impacts of steel tariffs.

The company was an important employer in its local area, producing steel canisters that it sold to a global slate of companies (so it was an exporter, and also sold domestically). Its main input was a particular type of steel pipe made in China (so it was also an importer). After Trump implemented steel tariffs, this small firm was suddenly paying an additional $250 million (back in 2018/2019; do your own inflation math as to what that would be today) at the US border before it could pick up a shipment.

It wasn’t going to be able to afford to stay open if it couldn’t get the administration to give it a tariff exemption (something Trump 1.0 was more willing to do, although the time involved to apply and, hopefully, get some sort of relief (many didn’t) meant companies were shelling out cash in the meantime). Why? Because not only did it not have a way to source the pipe in the US (steel is made to specification and you often can’t just readily swap things out), it couldn’t afford to do that because with a global client base, it needed to keep its pricing competitive (its customers could seek out non-US sources, unaffected by tariffs, for canisters instead).

We do actually have a manufacturing sector in the US. Most companies in that sector are small and midsized firms (fewer than 500 workers; often much smaller) and these may be important employers locally (although most employment in the industry overall is via the smaller number of very large firms); many are family firms. All sizes of manufacturer may import a raw material, a component or a finished good (including capital equipment for their facilities). When we tariff, we end up hurting our own manufacturing sector along the way. I lost track of the steel canister-maker’s fate, but I’ve never forgotten its difficulty, as just one illustration of tariff impacts that aren’t about the CPI.

But there’s also no real controversy (among people who study this stuff) in saying that tariffs tend to raise prices somewhere along the way, although it can take several months and may not be a straight $1 for $1 increase for end-consumers (although it often, eventually, is). I agree that it doesn’t create a prolonged rise in inflation (which is a rate of increase), but it does tend to eventually raise prices over a certain period and they then stay at that higher level. That’s actually part of how tariffs work, by putting a new floor under prices, reducing price competition.

And there are spillovers well beyond the firms initially impacted. For instance, US makers of tin plate, used in can-making, were hit by Trump 1.0’s steel tariffs, which jacked up their input costs (whether they continued with imports or switched to domestic sources — especially since domestic steel makers raised their own prices after tariffs were imposed on imports, an approach they’ve continued with in the latest trade war). This then made foreign-produced end-products such as canned food more attractive, because the pricing was better due to the lower production costs for non-US producers of tin plate. In other words, not only did US tin plate manufacturers suffer, but so did their US customers, as those companies’ customers looked elsewhere. (Trump’s much-broader trade war this time could offset some of this, by making imported canned goods more expensive, as well, depending on how things play out, which, in turn, would affect things like grocery store margins, etc.)

I also want to add that one of the biggest problems worrying the manufacturing industry for years, including pre-pandemic, has been the difficulty firms often face in filling the jobs they already have, and the difficulty they expect to face in filling jobs they expect to have due to a looming wave of retirements. This is due to several reasons: a skills gap (applicants not having the desired skill-sets); geographic miss-matches (jobs in one place, potential workers in another); problems with drug use in some communities (applicants are often expected to pass drug tests in order to operate machinery; the opioid epidemic has truly clobbered some communities in manufacturing areas); lack of interest among younger people in going into manufacturing or other production sectors (definitely something we need to work on; lack of exposure and training in K-12 is part of the trouble there, although the appeal of other types of work has also pulled potential workers elsewhere — maybe AI taking white collar jobs will sort that out?); and an increasing tightness in the overall US labor market due to demographics (ie, retirements on the aggregate, although jobs involving manual labor often see retirements at earlier ages, skewing the problem for those industries).

To finally conclude this overlong comment — which still barely scratches the surface; I didn’t even go into the tariff (and trade war) impacts on US shipping and logistics sectors tied to global trade, including imports — a major and rarely-discussed downside of tariffs is simply that it’s so difficult to readily see the ways they thread through an economy and create a drag on firms’ employment, wages/benefits, expansion plans, financing options, earnings and stock prices, and, yes, on consumer spending. The hits to businesses are often below the radar — especially since many companies don’t want to attract the anger of protectionists (unions; certain parts of the progressive wing; the Trump administration) by openly admitting how tariffs hurt their business. So people who aren’t trade geeks are understandably oblivious to real effects of these types of policies. As Cullen Roche over at Discipline Funds has repeatedly put it, with tariffs, you have less economic growth than you would have had — you just don’t know it.

The Biden administration and Dems in Congress (and sometimes even GOPers in Congress at that time, in some rare moments of bipartisanship) did several good things to directly support certain manufacturing and other production sectors (in my world I knew about policy for clean energy-related manufacturing; the defense industry; critical minerals; computer chips). Trump and the GOP have reduced or eliminated a chunk of that, unfortunately. But the recent tax bill did include some useful items for manufacturing. The GOP could do even more to directly support the sector, if manufacturing jobs are the real goal of all this, without the downsides of tariffs. (To be clear, this is not a political argument that I’m making; I didn’t like the tariffs imposed during the Biden admin, any more than Trump’s.)

This is an interesting analysis. The way I summed it up to an acquaintance is that Trump is playing with fire. In the end, it may be that we have something nice and shiny as a result. However, it is just as likely (if not more) that this whole thing is a dumpster fire and in the end it will just a smoking heap of ash.

However, the more fundamental problem here is that the reason that things like this (i.e., Trump unilaterally going tariff-nuclear, which is actually quite similar to what Biden did trying to illegally wipe out student loan debt, it’s just that Trump’s actions are at a different order of magnitude) is because Congress actively refuses to do their jobs. In the last several decades they have rather been rather determined to pass really loose/broad laws and specifically leave the “details” to the executive branch (either as some nebulous presidential power, or via some rule-making provision for an executive agency). This was bad but not terrible as long as we were electing presidents who were within a standard deviation of the ‘center’ of the political spectrum. However, Trump is a major outlier, and now it is readily apparent that Congress’ approach of letting the executive branch decide most things for itself isn’t actually a really good idea.

Even going back to the difference between Trump’s use of tariffs and Biden’s student debt cancellation efforts, it is clear that Biden’s policy, while objectively of very dubious legality, didn’t move the macroeconomic needle. Trump’s policies, on the other hand, even if they turn out to be completely legal (which I’m not sure they will), are rather painful object lesson on why Congress needs to actually do their jobs with a bit more effort.

A stray bit of additional perspective: A good friend of mine lost a large swath of her extended family when covid churned through northern Italy in the first year of the pandemic. Communities in their area suffered terrible losses that upended the social fabric overall, in addition to the grief suffered by specific families.

This also happened in many parts of the US, with certain kinds of communities hit particularly hard (groups that tend to live with extended family were especially vulnerable; non-hispanic white middle- and upper-class America is least-likely to live that way, so people from that type of background may not have seen much of this directly).

Given what NYC itself went through early in that first year, it also wouldn’t surprise me if NYT staffers genuinely felt horrified at what was happening. My friends and colleagues living in NYC certainly felt that way, based on what they were seeing and experiencing directly themselves.

So yes, it’s absolutely true that all forms of heart disease combined remained the number one cause of death in both 2020 and 2021, followed by all cancers combined. But I suspect that many people whose families and communities were gutted by covid would agree with the NYT that the toll from that new cause of death was terrible, and that it was something worth being concerned about, even if covid alone ended up being the third-leading cause of US deaths in both of those years, after which broad herd immunity finally set in.

Also, if anyone has an idea for how to fund newspaper journalism such that eyeballs aren’t the thing, I know several very good journalists who would *love* to hear what it is. (Pricier subscriptions can’t be the answer; not if you want to pay decent salaries and thus keep people around so that you have a good mix of entry-level people and experienced folks, and not if you want to include small and regional news outlets in your funding model — you could never charge enough for subscriptions for a local or even regional paper for that to cover all costs and still have a decent staff, both in terms of actual size and experience mix. This applies to both digital and hard-copy papers.)

If you do not think that the NYT serves a political agenda, the you are naïve.

And while I think that Pete’s nostalgic comment (“Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us…”) is equally naïve, he recognizes that today news organizations are driven by getting eyeballs on their content. The thing is, it’s always been like this. Certainly, the intensity has varied with times and places, but yellow journalism (the type of sensationalism that characterizes nearly 100% of mass media coverage today) originated in the 1880s in NYC. Back then the NYT didn’t lower themselves to that level, but it’s pretty obvious that today they are down there and they deserve to be compared to the likes of FoxNews, MSNBC, and so forth.

I think a useful comparison that illustrates something important about the NYT is to look at its news articles and compare them with those in the Wall Street Journal (owned by News Corp, by the way, as is Fox News). Both the NYT and WSJ are dealing with a crazy-ass environment for “newspapers” vs back in the day. And both approach their news journalism in a similar way, even if the specific type of news story they do may differ.

At the same time, nothing could be more different than their respective opinion sections — both the editorials by their editorial boards and those by columnists and guests are 180-degrees opposite from each other much of the time.

In other words, in terms of political-ish stance, they are radically different. In terms of journalism? Pretty similar: fact-based, attempting to give a full picture, and corrections if someone messes something up. They entertain if they can, but it’s secondary to information provision.

I can’t say the same about Fox News (which I used to watch some years ago, but stopped when I realized I was never really going to get a full picture of anything since it wasn’t their style). They are really an entertainment-first entity, and they are facing fierce competition from Newsmax, which has made it less and less appealing for them to say anything they think their viewers might not want to hear. (That said, I’ve found the online version of their sister product, Fox Business, to be helpful at times. Just as I like CNBC’s “state of freight” pages for some aspects of tariff impacts on shipping and warehousing. Written! Not the videos/cable shows for either of these. There’s usually more information in written material, and the potential for more nuance. (Not always fulfilled, alas).)

I think that there is a case to be made that sales taxes, above all other taxes, are the most “just” taxes. The idea is that sales taxes are the form of taxes that give the individual tax payer the greatest degree of economic freedom. Don’t want to pay so much in taxes? Then just buy less stuff!

This sort of thing is very difficult with other forms of taxes, because there aren’t reasonable ways to reduce property taxes, and in some cases (i.e., gentrification) your taxes can increase by huge amounts even if you do nothing at all but sit at home. Income taxes, excise taxes, and tariffs live in a bit of a middle ground (they provide a bit more economic freedom, but are still more difficult than sales taxes to deal with in terms of accomplishing the “I want to pay less tax” objective).

I agree wholeheartedly. Income tax punishes you for working. Nobody helped you, but you now owe a dramatically higher amount of tax. Extreme (and rare) example, but illustrates how bizarre this type of taxation is. And of course, if you are renting, and the property owner’s assessment goes up, this is going to be passed on with a rent increase unless there is a rent control law, which will lead to a dilapidated building in need of repair, or people leaving the area, and many other problems.

With all due respect, you, and unfortunately, many others, are missing the point.

We (and Trump) get that the cost will get passed onto the consumers. Or at least that’s the “first order effect” (to borrow your phrase.)

What you’re missing is that consumers get to decide between whether to purchase the item or not. If they are willing to eat the cost, and the item is something they absolutely can’t live without, they’ll buy it. Or they won’t buy it at all.

In the latter case, the sales numbers (and thus revenue) of the company selling the goods will drop. At which point that company has a choice to make: live with the drop in sales, and thus bottom line, eat part of the tariff or all of it, in order to increase volume.

Obviously, the company’s goal (let’s use Nike as an example), is to make as much money as possible. So if they naively pass 100% of the cost onto the consumer, their sales might drop so much that they’ll realize that wasn’t the best financial decision. This is an optimization problem: find the global maximum. The variables are: what % of tariffs to eat (vs pass on), whether to continue to offshore or onshore (and to what degree), and so on.

Using the Nike example (because they recently sobbed about their $1Bn tariff bill), their product is, among other things, athletic shoes. They’re not an essential item. They’re a luxury. It’s also not something you buy every week. Consumers can easily forego purchasing a new pair of Nike shoes, and Nike can decide if it can stomach the sales drop or not and react accordingly. That’s not our concern. We shouldn’t feel sorry for Nike who got rich at the expense of exploiting sweat job labor and pocketing the enormous margins, while selling out American jobs.

The other second-order effect you missed is the fact that by creating these “tariff walls” the money stays onshore. I.e. customers buy US-made goods and pay local companies, i.e. their fellow citizen. The money feeds back into the US economy. Without them, even though goods are “cheaper” for the consumer, the money flows out of the country: enriching China and other third world countries at our expense. What are some third-order effects you think might arise from that? I hope you see how this thinking is a bit short-sighted.

#8435. How to Skin a Deer Like a Pro

Published Oct 26, 2026 9:38 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

If you ask a dozen hunters how to skin a deer, you’ll find that every one of them does something slightly different. While that may be frustrating for newer hunters, it should also be reassuring: There’s no one right way or right order to skin a deer. As long as you follow the general techniques and handy tips outlined below, you’ll be able to skin a deer in no time.

Once you do get the hang of it, skinning a deer is quick and easy. Butchering and packaging a deer can take all afternoon but “if it takes me 10 minutes to skin a deer,” says Cheyne Matzenbacher, a one-time deer processor and current deer outreach specialist for the National Deer Association, “that’s a long time.”

Read through the whole article or click on a topic below to jump ahead.

Although there are lots of tools and setups that can make skinning a deer much easier, the only thing you really need is a sharp knife. The best skinning knives are typically handy enough for maneuvering but durable enough for joint work. There’s nothing wrong with using a small folding skinning knife in the backcountry or a longer filet knife. Just don’t use a dull knife — it’s dangerous and takes longer to finish the job.

Before you can skin your deer, you need to gut or field dress your deer, which involves removing the internal organs from the chest and abdominal cavities. Once your deer is gutted, you’ll ideally want to hang it. It’s certainly possible to skin your deer on the ground or the bed of your pickup (I’ve done both many times), and if you plan to do this, you should study up on the gutless method of skinning deer and other big game. This process is preferred by backcountry hunters who quarter their deer in the field, slip the meat into game bags, and pack it back to camp or their trucks.

But for most whitetail hunters and Western hunters who hunt close to home, it’s easier and faster to skin a deer that’s hanging. The meat will also stay cleaner if it’s hanging instead of touching dirt, bacteria, and deer hair on, say, your tailgate. There are a dozen methods for hanging a deer, and they all depend on your location and the tools available to you.

Deer hunters are divided on this question. You can skin a deer that’s hanging head up or head down, but there are advantages to each method. When Matzenbacher worked as a deer processor for a season, he and his coworkers would hang deer by the head or neck to skin the animal, then flip it to hang head-down for butchering.

“Think about how a deer jumps over a fence: His legs are folded up against his body. Let gravity help you, and let the natural way a deer is going to fold up help you skin it,” says Matzenbacher. “Don’t fight it.”

I skin all my deer head-down, so that’s how I’ll walk you through this example. If you want to try the head-up method, the principles are all the same. Just start at the neck and work your way down. If you are planning to shoulder mount your deer, don’t follow all of these instructions; you’ll need to make very careful cuts near the forelegs and chest. These traditional instructions are for does or for bucks you plan to skull cap or Euro mount. Finally, redneck ingenuity abounds when it comes to skinning deer, and if you’re interested in working smarter, not harder, consider the golf-ball trick or skinning your deer with your truck.

Make identical circular cuts near the knee joints, circling the thin bone of the lower leg on the side closer to the hoof. (This is the only time you should be cutting down on deer hair. For all the rest of the cuts, insert your knife under the hide and cut parallel to the meat or away from the meat.)

Slip the tip of your knife under the hide inside one hind leg. Applying even pressure, cut up and out in a single smooth motion as you run your blade toward the pelvis until you reach the cut you made while field dressing. Do this on the other hind leg, then start to skin the hide away from the tendons where you’re going to put the gambrel and expose the knees. The idea is to remove just enough hide that you don’t have to skin around the metal of the gambrel once you hang the deer.

Thread the gambrel through the natural holes you just exposed in the hind legs (between the bone and thick tendon) and hoist your deer. Tie it off at a comfortable height to work on the hindquarters

Note: You can perform this at almost any point in the process. Some hunters prefer to do this before hanging their deer, others do it as needed throughout the process (as pictured). You can also use loppers or a reciprocating saw for this and may want a saw for the hind legs; just take care not to cut the big tendon on the hind legs.

Slightly bend the front legs and cut through the joint. Wiggle the leg to find the weakest point and use your knife blade to cut perpendicularly through the tendons and between the bones until the joint is free. This may seem tricky at first, but it’s simpler than it looks.

Run your knife between the lower leg cuts and the cut along the abdomen you made while field dressing. Do this on both sides of the inner hindquarters. Combined with the lower leg cuts (or removal) these are the major cuts that will allow you to skin most of your deer.

Using your off hand to lift the hide and your knife hand to make cuts parallel to the meat, begin to peel away the hide. Work from the inside of the hind leg around to the outside. Do this on both sides.

Separate the hide at the tail by either running your knife under the hide and pulling it off the tail like yanking off a sock, or cutting the tail off altogether. Use your knife to work between the joints or simply saw it off.

Now you can begin the easiest part of skinning a deer: letting gravity help you pull the hide off. You may need to raise the deer a little for this part. Once you’ve used your knife to separate the hide from the tail and the inside of the hind legs, set it aside and grab fist-fulls of hide. Using your body weight, pull the hide toward the ground. If the hide doesn’t pull free in places, you can use your knife to help release the hide by slicing the delicate white crackly tissue that connects the skin to the meat. You’ll likely need to do this around the belly area and occasionally along the back

The hide will start to form a tube as you peel it away and it gets closer to the chest and neck.

Before the hide gets in your way too much and starts to drape over the forelegs, make cuts inside the forelegs similar to the ones you made on the hindlegs, starting near the knee joint and running the blade along the backs of the legs until they reach the body and chest. (If you didn’t remove the lower forelegs before, be sure to do this before you try to pull the hide over it.) You can also just pull the skin over the forelegs by pushing down on the hide between the brisket and front of the cut front legs (see video above). It’s similar to pulling off a sock.

Continue to work the hide down over the shoulders and forelegs like you’re peeling off a sweatshirt. The cuts you made on the legs will appear and you can use your knife to free the hide.

Once the hide is over the shoulders, use your knife to separate it from the neck. The freed hide will be heavy now and starting to get in your way. Use its weight to your advantage so it pulls the at the hide still connected to the deer.

When you reach the base of the neck, use a saw or your knife to sever the head from the vertebrae. You’ll have to cut through meat and tendons on all sides until you reach the spine. If you’re using a knife, work through the vertebrae like you did with the knee joints, turning the deer’s head a little bit to help free space between the vertebrae. You want to make your cut at the atlas joint, the connection between the head and the first vertebra of the neck and spinal column.

Once you cut through the neckbone the hide should be completely removed from your deer, though still attached to the head. If you need to get your deer tested for CWD or plan to make a European mount, just slice away all that extra hide hanging off the head.

This step is only necessary if you plan to make your own skull mount. Start at the neck and cut away the skin as you did on the rest of the deer, making cuts parallel to the meat and skull until you’ve removed most of the skin. A flathead screwdriver can help free the hide at the base of a buck’s pedicles, which can be the trickiest part to remove. This is a more time consuming process and should be done carefully to avoid injury or scoring the skull with your knife, which can cause cosmetic damage.

No, you don’t have to hang a deer to skin it. I’ve skinned plenty of deer in the back of a pickup, and sometimes that’s your only option if you’re hunting in areas without many trees or access to a barn or meat pole. It’s definitely easier to skin a deer if it’s hanging since gravity helps remove the hide. It’s also easier to keep the meat clean if your deer is hanging when you skin it; skinning a deer on a level surface like a tailgate or outdoor table makes it more likely that you’ll get deer hair and possibly dirt or bacteria on the meat.

The only tool you must have to skin a deer is a reasonably sharp knife. There are plenty of additional tools that make the job easier, and those will depend on where you’re skinning your deer. If you’re working in the field, consider a hitch hoist for your vehicle and a pair of loppers to quickly remove legs. If you have the luxury of a garage, shed, or barn to hang your deer, along with electricity, you might invest in an electric winch and a Sawzall.

How fast you need to skin a deer depends on a few factors, including the temperature outside and your state’s carcass transportation laws. As a general rule, in the right conditions (cool and dry), a deer can hang hide-on for several weeks. (See below for more details.) If it’s hot and humid, skin the deer as fast as you can to help cool the meat and prevent spoilage. If temperatures are near or below freezing, you should skin a deer while the carcass is still warm and the hide is pliable; skinning a frozen deer is both difficult and time consuming. Meanwhile, CWD laws in your state may require you to debone all deer meat before crossing county or state lines. If such regulations apply where you hunt or live, you’re going to need to skin your deer so you can debone it before you hit the road.

A skinned deer can hang for up to a few weeks if it’s stored in the proper conditions. The deer needs to stay cool and dry, such as sheltered outside during the winter or (preferably) inside a walk-in cooler set to a consistent temperature. Experts recommend hanging deer for 7 to 10 days at a temperature between 35 and 45 degrees to allow enzymes to age, or tenderize, the meat. A deer will not age properly if it’s frozen.

Yes, you can age deer meat with the skin on. Opinions on this vary about which method (aging venison with or without the hide) is better. Any meat that’s exposed to air as it ages will develop a dried crust, and the hide can help protect that meat from drying. I once hung a doe, hide-on, in a walk in-cooler with the temperature set to 38 degrees for two weeks. It was surprisingly easy to skin after aging and I lost less meat than when I age completely skinned quarters. But if you let your deer hang for much longer than that (three weeks or more) the meat may over-tenderize and start to come away with the hide, forcing you to work slowly and possibly wasting meat. Still, letting deer meat hang for at least a day or more can help keep it dry, tenderize the venison, and concentrate flavor before butchering.

The best deer skinning knife is a sharp one. The type of knife—skinning, caping, boning, or filet—matters less than its sharpness and the cuts you make. Many hunters and wild game processors prefer different types of knives for different stages of the skinning process: There are skinning knives (usually slim, handy knives with a sturdy blade), flexible filet knives for working around awkward angles or different muscle groups, caping knives for skinning the shoulders and head of a trophy deer, and stout boning knives for separating knee joints. Try several types of knives to find the best deer skinning knife for you.

Remember, there is no single perfect way to skin a deer. Every deer hunter and processor I’ve met does something slightly different, and most swear their way is the best way. Find which tools and techniques work for how you hunt and what kind of facilities you have access to (if any). The only way to truly learn how to skin a deer is, well, to skin a deer. So sharpen your knife and get after it.

#8434. Give Each Goal the Account Built for It – 401(k), IRA, HSA, 529 & Brokerage

Pick the investment account by what the money is for, because the account decides how it’s taxed and when you can withdraw it. Use a 401(k) or IRA for retirement, a health savings account for medical bills, a 529 plan for education, and a taxable brokerage account for other long-term goals.

Pick the wrong one and it costs you later, in tax you could have avoided or a penalty for taking money out early.

A traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account (IRA) can cut your taxable income now, and you pay income tax on withdrawals in retirement. A Roth 401(k) or IRA does the reverse. You pay tax on what goes in, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free. Choosing between a Roth and a traditional IRA comes down to whether you expect a higher tax rate now or in retirement. You can put in up to $24,500 a year in a 401(k) and $7,500 across your traditional and Roth IRAs combined, with higher limits from age 50. Most withdrawals before age 59½ also cost a 10% penalty on top of any income tax.

A health savings account (HSA) is tax-free going in, while it grows, and coming out for qualified medical expenses. You can fund one only while you’re covered by an HSA-eligible health plan, such as one with a high deductible. A 529 plan grows tax-free and pays out tax-free for college and other qualified school costs, though what you put in isn’t deductible on your federal return. A taxable brokerage account has no tax break, but also no limits or withdrawal rules. You pay tax on its dividends each year and on gains when you sell.

You don’t need all five at once. Fill them in this order: your 401(k) up to any match your employer offers, then a Roth IRA or an HSA, then more 401(k) or a taxable account. A full financial order of operations also places debt payoff and an emergency fund among those steps.

A 28-year-old with no 401(k) who’s saving for retirement and for a down payment in four years needs two places, a Roth IRA for retirement and a high-yield savings account for the down payment.

Money you’ll need within about five years belongs in savings, not stocks, because a market drop right before you spend it could leave you short.

#8432. Free Stock Is Real Money – Use It to Break a Tie Between Brokers

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Free stock from a broker is real money, but a sign-up share is often worth a few dollars. The broker you pick may hold your investments for decades. Shortlist online brokers by their costs, the funds they sell, and the account you need, then take a free-stock offer only from a broker on your shortlist.

A sign-up share pays you once. The broker’s fees and choice of funds affect you every year you stay, and any charge for moving your account out comes due the day you leave.

You can get free stock four ways. Brokers give shares to new customers who open or fund an account, as Webull’s free-share offer does, and to current customers who refer friends. Stash’s Stock-Back debit card pays rewards in stock, and Acorns invests the rewards you earn shopping with its partner brands.

The shares tend to be small, and they come with conditions. Robinhood’s sign-up stock is worth $5 to $200, and about 99% of new customers get the minimum. You can sell the share after 3 trading days, but you can’t withdraw its cash value for 60 days. It also comes only with an individual taxable account, not an individual retirement account (IRA). Any tax on it is yours, and its value may show up on a 1099 tax form.

Skipping that order can turn a free share into a loss. Say you take an $8 share from a broker that doesn’t carry the funds you want and charges $75 to transfer an account out. Paying the fee to move the account leaves you $67 behind. A fractional free share, a slice of one share, can’t transfer to another broker, the brokerage regulator FINRA notes, so you’d have to sell it first.

Take a free share only from a broker you’d have opened without it.

Find that broker among the best online brokers for beginners.

#8430. Investing in Your 20s – Take the Match, Open a Roth IRA, and Own Stocks

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Money you invest in your 20s has about 40 years to grow, so small amounts go far. Contribute enough to your 401(k) to get the full employer match, open a Roth IRA while your tax rate is low, and invest both accounts mostly in stocks through a target-date or broad stock index fund.

Starting early can matter more than the amount you put in, since money you invest at 25 gets 10 more years to compound than money you invest at 35.

A Roth IRA suits your 20s. You pay income tax on what you put in at today’s rate, and in retirement the money and its growth come out tax-free. That trade pays off most when your tax rate is low, and on a first salary it’s likely the lowest it will be in your career.

With about 40 years until retirement, you can hold mostly stocks, which swing more than bonds but have historically grown more. If the market drops 30% when you’re 25, every contribution buys shares for 30% less while prices stay down, and you won’t need to sell for decades. Keep buying through it.

Take the steps in this order. First, get the full match, the money your employer adds when you contribute, as soon as your plan allows. Build a starter emergency fund, a small cash cushion for surprise bills, at the same time. Next, pay off any high-interest debt, such as a credit card balance. Then, if your income is under the IRS’s ceiling for Roth contributions, open a Roth IRA and contribute up to the yearly limit, $7,500. Anything past that goes back into your 401(k).

In both accounts, pick a low-cost target-date fund named for the year you plan to retire. It holds mostly stocks while that year is far off and shifts toward bonds as it nears. A broad stock index fund, which owns small slices of hundreds or thousands of companies, works too.

At a hypothetical 7% average annual return, raising your contributions from 6% to 10% of a $50,000 salary adds $2,000 a year that grows to about $400,000 over 40 years. So each time your pay goes up, save another 1% or 2% of it until you and your employer together put in 15% of your pay.

To choose a firm for your Roth IRA, compare the best places to open an IRA.

Picture this: you're settling into a lie-flat business class seat somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of something cold in hand, knowing that in 48 hours you'll be waking up in Istanbul — and then, a few days later, continuing onward to Bangkok. Two bucket-list cities. One award booking. One points balance. This is what the Aeroplan stopover sweet spot feels like in practice. It's not a trick or a loophole — it's a deliberately designed feature of Air Canada's Aeroplan program that the vast majority of travelers simply don't know exists. And that gap between awareness and reality is exactly where the ChooseFI community finds its edge. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class itinerary from North America to Istanbul with a continuing flight onward to Bangkok — two long-haul segments, lie-flat seats, Star Alliance lounges at every connection — would cost somewhere between **$6,000 and $15,000 in cash**. That's a realistic retail range depending on season and how far out you book. Most people never consider it a possibility for a family vacation or a milestone trip because the sticker price puts it in a different universe. With Aeroplan, you're booking that same itinerary — the same seats, the same lounges, the same Turkish Airlines or Thai Airways product — for **75,000 Aeroplan points**. At the low end of the cash price range, that's already **8 cents per point**. At the high end, you're extracting **20 cents per point** from a currency that most people earned by putting groceries on a credit card. The pricing inefficiency here is structural. Aeroplan's partner award chart prices long-haul business class at a fixed rate regardless of cash fare fluctuations. When business class prices spike — around holidays, during peak travel seasons, during major events — your points cost stays exactly the same. You're insulated from the market. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: you've already paid for the trip in points, slowly accumulated through everyday spending, and now you're simply redeeming the stored value. The stopover itself is nearly free. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 extra miles to add a stopover city to a one-way award. That means your Istanbul layover becomes a multi-day stay — at zero additional points cost beyond that small add-on — and you haven't booked a second award at all. One booking. Two destinations. That's the entire premise, and once you see it, you can't unsee it.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you understand it, but it requires knowing three things that most travelers don't: how Aeroplan's routing rules work, what a stopover actually is in the context of an award ticket, and why Star Alliance's global network makes this scalable to almost any destination pair you can imagine.

When Aeroplan relaunched its loyalty program in 2020, it did something remarkable: it eliminated fuel surcharges entirely and published a partner award chart with fixed pricing for flights on Star Alliance carriers. This is critical. When you book Turkish Airlines business class through Aeroplan, you pay the Aeroplan fixed chart rate — not what Turkish Airlines would charge in its own currency or miles program, and not the inflated cash price. That fixed chart is the engine of this redemption.

For long-haul international business class, Aeroplan's chart prices routing through multiple regions based on your origin and destination — not every intermediate stop. This is the aha moment. Aeroplan determines your award price based on where your journey starts and where it ends, and then allows you to add a stopover in between for just 5,000 additional miles. The stopover city is priced as a pass-through for the purpose of calculating your award zone, not as a second trip.

On a one-way Aeroplan award, you're permitted to add a free stopover — meaning you can stay in an intermediate city for any length of time before continuing to your final destination. That 5,000-mile add-on is essentially the cost of a full additional destination. Compare that to booking a second one-way award from Istanbul to Bangkok, which would cost you another 40,000–55,000 Aeroplan points in business class. The math is decisive.

The routing must be geographically sensible — you can't fly backwards across the globe — but Aeroplan's allowance for multi-segment itineraries through Star Alliance hubs gives you enormous flexibility. Istanbul (IST) is a Turkish Airlines hub. Bangkok (BKK) is served by Thai Airways and several Star Alliance carriers. Both are Star Alliance partners. Both are bookable through Aeroplan at fixed chart rates with no fuel surcharges.

The best part for the ChooseFI community is how accessible the underlying points are. Aeroplan accepts transfers from four major programs:

Chase's instant transfer speed is particularly valuable here. When you find business class availability — which can disappear quickly — you want to move points immediately. Having Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency means you can search, find space, and transfer points before the availability window closes. The 1:1 ratio across all four programs means no conversion math — every point you earn translates directly to one Aeroplan mile.

Booking an Aeroplan stopover award in business class is genuinely one of the more complex redemptions in the travel rewards world, but it becomes manageable when you break it into distinct phases. Here's exactly how to do it.

Start by deciding on your two destinations. Aeroplan stopovers work best when your intermediate city is a major Star Alliance hub that lies geographically between your origin and final destination. Classic combinations include North America to Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub) continuing to Southeast Asia, or North America to a European hub continuing to the Middle East or East Africa. Your stopover city should be somewhere you genuinely want to spend 2–5 days — this is a real trip, not just a layover.

This is the most important and most time-consuming step. You need to find saver-level business class availability on both segments independently before you book.

Once you've confirmed availability on both segments, go to aeroplan.com and use the multi-city search function. Enter your full itinerary — origin, stopover city with your intended layover dates, and final destination.

Once you've confirmed the award is bookable and are ready to complete the reservation:

Complete your booking on aeroplan.com or with a phone agent, confirm the stopover is properly reflected in your itinerary, and save every confirmation email. Verify your seats on each carrier's website immediately after booking.

A stopover is an intentional break in your journey lasting more than 24 hours at a connecting city. Most airlines treat stopovers as separate tickets, charging full price for each segment. Aeroplan is one of the few programs that allows a free stopover on round-trip awards, letting you explore a connecting city for days before continuing to your final destination. This is fundamentally different from a layover, which is a brief connection of a few hours at an airport. The stopover must be in a city served by a Star Alliance carrier on your routing, and the key is that Aeroplan prices the entire itinerary as one award, not two.

Let's build a real example so you can see exactly what this looks like on paper — and in the air.

The Route: Toronto (YYZ) → Istanbul (IST, 4-day stopover) → Bangkok (BKK) The Carrier: Turkish Airlines business class on both segments The Points Cost: 75,000 Aeroplan miles for the two segments + 5,000 miles for the stopover = 80,000 Aeroplan miles total Cash Equivalent: A comparable business class itinerary on this routing typically retails for $9,000–$12,000 in 2026, depending on when you search and how far in advance you book.

The CPP Calculation: At the midpoint cash value of $10,500 against 80,000 points, you're extracting 13.1 cents per Aeroplan mile — well inside the 8–20 cent range this sweet spot delivers, and roughly 10–13 times the value of redeeming Aeroplan miles for cash back.

The Turkish Airlines business class product on long-haul routes is consistently rated among the top business class experiences in the Star Alliance network. On the YYZ–IST segment — operated on a 787 or A330 — you'll have access to a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, the Turkish Airlines Lounge in Istanbul (widely considered one of the best airport lounges in the world, full stop), and a meal service that reflects the airline's culinary reputation. The IST lounge alone — with its restaurant, spa, golf simulator, and sleeping areas — is worth lingering in even before your onward connection.

In Istanbul, your four days might include the Hagia Sophia at sunrise, a Bosphorus dinner cruise, and the Grand Bazaar before you head to the airport to continue your journey. You've paid nothing additional for this stay beyond the 5,000-mile stopover fee.

The IST–BKK segment puts you into Bangkok in the evening, ready for Thailand's extraordinary food, culture, and cost of living — which, for the FI-minded traveler, means your lodging and meals on the ground are remarkably affordable, stretching the value of your trip even further.

Total points cost for two lie-flat business class segments and a full European city stay: 80,000 miles, earned on everyday credit card spending. That's the entire proposition, and those numbers are real.
